children.title: Why Data Preprocessing Is Needed
children.body:
Real-World Data Is Rarely Clean

Databases built for day-to-day operations are designed to record transactions, not to support analysis. They contain missing fields, wrong entries, duplicate records, inconsistent codes and values recorded in different units. Data mining algorithms assume that the input describes the problem faithfully, so dirty input produces models that look precise but are wrong. This is the well-known garbage in, garbage out (GIGO) problem.

  • Incomplete: a customer record has no age or income because the field was optional or the value was unknown.
  • Noisy: a sensor records 21.7 C, 21.9 C and then 41.7 C because of a transmission error.
  • Inconsistent: the same city is stored as "Bengaluru", "Bangalore" and "BLR"; a date is stored as 03/04/2024 in one table and 2024-04-03 in another.
  • Redundant: both date of birth and age are stored, so one of them is almost always out of date.
  • Wrong type or scale: salary is a text field with "40k", "40000" and "40,000" in different rows.

Data Quality Dimensions

DimensionQuestion it answersExample of failure
AccuracyIs the value correct?Age = 210 for a student
CompletenessAre all required values present?40% of income fields empty
ConsistencyDo related values agree?Age 25 but date of birth says 1970
TimelinessIs the value current?Address from five years ago
BelievabilityIs the source trustworthy?Self-reported weight in a medical study
InterpretabilityIs the meaning clear?A column named "flag" with values 1/2/9

Where Preprocessing Sits in the KDD Process

Preprocessing is the step between data selection and data mining in the knowledge discovery process. It is usually the most time-consuming stage: practitioners often report that 60 to 80 percent of the total effort in a real project goes into understanding, cleaning and shaping the data.

raw sources
   |  data selection
   v
selected data
   |  data cleaning + integration + transformation + reduction
   v
prepared data
   |  data mining
   v
patterns
   |  interpretation and evaluation
   v
knowledge

Why "Just Mine It" Fails

  • A decision tree trained on data with 30 percent missing income simply splits on "income = unknown" and learns nothing useful.
  • A classifier trained on a dataset where the target is encoded two different ways treats one class as two and reports a false accuracy.
  • A clustering algorithm dominated by a salary column ranging from 10,000 to 10,000,000 puts every record in one cluster because one attribute overwhelms the distance.
  • Duplicate records make a support count for an association rule look twice as strong as it really is.

Exam point: define the four classic data quality problems (incomplete, noisy, inconsistent, redundant) with one example each, then explain that preprocessing improves mining quality and reduces mining time.

children.title: Major Tasks of Data Preprocessing
children.body:
The Five Main Tasks

Data preprocessing is usually described as five cooperating tasks. Real pipelines mix and repeat them, but an exam answer should present them in this order and say what each one fixes.

  • Data cleaning: fill in missing values, smooth noise, identify or remove outliers, and resolve inconsistencies. Fixes incomplete and noisy data.
  • Data integration: combine data from multiple databases, files or services into one coherent store, resolving entity conflicts and redundancy. Fixes fragmented and duplicated data.
  • Data transformation: convert data into forms suitable for mining: smoothing, aggregation, generalisation, attribute construction, normalisation and discretisation.
  • Data reduction: obtain a smaller representation that produces almost the same mining result: dimensionality reduction, numerosity reduction and compression.
  • Discretisation and concept hierarchies: replace continuous values by intervals and raw values by higher-level concepts (street to city to state to country).

Task, Problem and Typical Techniques

TaskProblem solvedTypical techniques
CleaningMissing values, noise, outliers, inconsistencyMean/mode imputation, binning, regression, clustering, deduplication
IntegrationMultiple sources, conflicting names and unitsSchema matching, entity resolution, correlation analysis, metadata
TransformationValues on the wrong scale or in the wrong formMin-max and z-score normalisation, log transform, aggregation, attribute construction
ReductionToo many rows or columns for the algorithmPCA, attribute subset selection, histograms, sampling, data cube aggregation
DiscretisationContinuous attributes where nominal ones are neededEqual-width and equal-frequency binning, entropy-based splits, chi-merge

Typical Pipeline

raw data
  -> data cleaning        (fill, smooth, remove duplicates)
  -> data integration     (join sources, resolve entities)
  -> data transformation  (scale, aggregate, construct attributes)
  -> data reduction       (fewer rows / fewer columns)
  -> discretisation       (intervals, concept hierarchies)
  -> mining algorithm

The order is not sacred. Reduction before transformation is common when the dataset is huge, and discretisation is sometimes treated as part of transformation. What matters is that each step is documented so the mining result can be reproduced.

Why Reduction Matters

A dataset with a million rows and two thousand attributes can take hours or days to mine and may overfit. Reduction keeps the information that matters: a 30-attribute subset chosen by information gain, a 95 percent variance-preserving PCA projection, or a stratified sample of 50,000 rows can give nearly the same model in a fraction of the time.

Exam point: list the five tasks, state the problem each solves and give one technique per task. A small pipeline diagram plus one concrete example (for instance, cleaning a customer table before churn prediction) earns full marks.

children.title: Missing Values: Mechanisms and Handling
children.body:
Why Values Go Missing

  • The value was not recorded: the field is optional, or the form was incomplete.
  • The value exists but is unavailable at mining time: a sensor was offline, a partner database was not joined.
  • The value does not apply: "number of children" is empty for a person with none.
  • The value was lost during integration: a join did not match, or a code was mapped to nothing.
  • The value was rejected as invalid and blanked: age = -3 was replaced by empty.

Mechanisms of Missingness

MechanismMeaningExample
MCAR (missing completely at random)Missingness is unrelated to any value, observed or unobservedA page of a survey is lost
MAR (missing at random)Missingness depends on observed variables onlyYounger respondents skip the income question
MNAR (missing not at random)Missingness depends on the missing value itselfHigh earners refuse to state income

MCAR and MAR can be handled by principled imputation with little bias. MNAR is dangerous: ignoring it creates a biased sample, and the bias cannot be removed from the data alone.

Handling Methods

  • Ignore the tuple: drop rows with missing values. Simple, but loses information and can bias the sample when missingness is not MCAR.
  • Ignore the attribute: drop a column that is missing almost everywhere. Useful when the column carries little information.
  • Fill with a global constant: "unknown", 0 or -1. Fast, but teaches the model a fake value and distorts statistics.
  • Fill with a central value: mean for numeric, median for skewed numeric, mode for categorical.
  • Fill with a class-conditional value: the mean income of the same class (for example, per churn label). Better than a global mean when the class is known.
  • Predictive imputation: regress the missing attribute on the other attributes, or use a decision tree, k-NN or expectation maximisation to estimate it.
  • Add an indicator: keep the imputed value and add a binary "was missing" column so the model can learn the pattern of missingness.
  • Multiple imputation: generate several plausible complete datasets, mine each, and combine the results. Most statistically sound, most expensive.

Worked Example

Age column with two missing values: 22, -, 25, -, 40, 22.

MethodValue usedResulting column
Mean(22 + 25 + 40 + 22) / 4 = 27.2522, 27.25, 25, 27.25, 40, 22
Medianbetween 22 and 25 = 23.522, 23.5, 25, 23.5, 40, 22
Mode22 (appears twice)22, 22, 25, 22, 40, 22
Class-conditional meanmean within the same class, e.g. 26.022, 26, 25, 26, 40, 22

Pitfalls

  • Mean imputation shrinks variance and weakens correlations, so models look more confident than they are.
  • Imputing before splitting into training and test sets leaks test information into training. Always fit the imputation on the training fold.
  • Filling a numeric column with 0 can be a valid measurement, so the model cannot distinguish "zero" from "unknown" unless an indicator is added.
  • MNAR data cannot be fixed by better imputation; you must model the missingness or collect the data differently.

Exam point: name the three mechanisms, then compare dropping rows, global constant, mean/mode, class-conditional mean and predictive imputation. Mention the bias and variance trade-offs.

children.title: Noisy Data: Binning, Regression and Clustering
children.body:
What Noise Is

Noise is a random error or variance in a measured value: a corrupted digit, a transmission glitch, a misread sensor or a typo. An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data; it may be noise or a genuine rare event. Cleaning removes noise while trying not to delete real extremes.

  • Instrument error: a thermometer reads 41.7 C instead of 21.7 C.
  • Human entry error: a salary typed as 900000 instead of 90000.
  • Transmission error: a dropped digit during data transfer.
  • Inconsistent formatting: "1,20,000" and "120000" treated as different values.

Binning (Discretisation Smoothing)

Sort the values, divide them into equal-frequency bins and replace every value in a bin by a representative value. Sorted data: 4, 8, 15, 21, 21, 24, 25, 28, 34. With three bins of three values each:

BinValuesBin meanBin medianBin boundaries
14, 8, 15984, 15
221, 21, 24222121, 24
325, 28, 34292825, 34

Smoothing by bin mean replaces 4, 8, 15 by 9, 9, 9; by bin median by 8, 8, 8; by bin boundaries, each value is moved to the nearer boundary, giving 4, 4, 15 and 21, 21, 24 and 25, 25, 34. Binning is simple and local, but it can destroy fine structure and the bin width is an arbitrary choice.

Regression Smoothing

Fit a model to the data and replace each value by the model prediction. For a straight line y = a + bx fitted to (x, y) pairs, noise is flattened while the trend is kept. Linear regression suits a global trend; multiple regression handles several predictors; a local regression (LOESS) fits a curve in a moving window.

y ^
  |        o
  |     o     o
  |  o    o
  | o  o
  +------------------> x
fitted line y = a + b x smooths the scatter

Clustering to Detect Outliers

Cluster the data; values that fall far from every cluster centre, or form a tiny cluster of their own, are candidates for noise or outliers. A common rule is to treat points more than three standard deviations from the mean, or outside 1.5 times the interquartile range, as outliers.

What to Do With an Outlier

ActionWhen it is appropriateRisk
Keep itGenuine rare event such as fraudModel chases rare cases
Remove itConfirmed data errorDeletes real signal if wrong
Cap (winsorise) itExtreme but plausible valueChanges the distribution
Separate itOutlier is a different populationNeeds a second model

Duplicates and Inconsistency

Noise also appears as duplicate rows and contradictory values. Exact duplicates are removed with a unique key or by comparing all fields. Near-duplicates need fuzzy matching on name, address or date. Contradictions (age 25 but birth year 1970) are resolved by a rule, a trusted source or manual review.

Exam point: be ready to smooth a given list of numbers by bin means, bin medians and bin boundaries. State that binning is a local smoothing method and that regression and clustering are alternatives.

children.title: Schema Integration and Redundancy
children.body:
What Integration Means

Data integration combines data from multiple sources into a coherent store. The sources may be relational databases, spreadsheets, web logs, sensors or purchased datasets. The hard part is not moving the bytes, it is deciding that a row in one table and a row in another talk about the same real-world object.

Entity Identification

Integration starts with schema integration: matching attributes from different schemas that describe the same concept. This requires a data dictionary or metadata that maps synonyms:

Source ASource BResolved to
customer.cust_idsales.client_codeentity Customer, key customer_id
emp.nameworker.full_nameattribute name
item.priceproduct.unit_costattribute price (but check units)
dtorder_dateattribute date

Matching by attribute name alone fails (two "amount" columns may mean price and discount). Matching by data values helps: two columns that mostly contain the same domain values are probably the same attribute. Full schema matching is a research problem; in practice, metadata and human review do most of the work.

Redundancy and Correlation Analysis

Redundancy means the same information is stored more than once. It can be an exact duplicate attribute or a derived attribute (date of birth plus age). Redundancy can also hide in statistically dependent attributes. Two tests are taught:

  1. Chi-square test (categorical pairs): compares observed counts with the counts expected if the two attributes were independent. A large chi-square value means the attributes are correlated.
  2. Correlation coefficient and covariance (numeric pairs): a value near +1 or -1 means strong linear dependence; near 0 means independence.

Chi-Square Worked Example

Whether a customer reads fiction vs non-fiction, by gender. Observed table (160 people):

FictionNon-fictionRow total
MaleA = 50B = 3080
FemaleC = 30D = 5080
Column total8080160

Expected value for each cell = row total x column total / grand total = 80 x 80 / 160 = 40.

chi-square = sum over cells (observed - expected)^2 / expected = (50-40)^2/40 + (30-40)^2/40 + (30-40)^2/40 + (50-40)^2/40 = 2.5 + 2.5 + 2.5 + 2.5 = 10. With (2-1)(2-1) = 1 degree of freedom, 10 is far above the critical value, so gender and reading preference are dependent and the attributes carry overlapping information.

Covariance and Correlation

cov(A, B) = [ sum(Ai - meanA)(Bi - meanB) ] / n
corr(A, B) = cov(A, B) / (sdA * sdB)

cov > 0 : both tend to be above (or below) their means together
cov < 0 : one is high while the other is low
cov = 0 : no linear relationship

Correlation is the normalised version, always between -1 and +1, so it compares pairs of attributes on different scales. If two attributes are highly correlated or perfectly covariant, one of them is redundant and can be dropped.

Exam point: compute chi-square for a small contingency table, compute covariance for a few points, and interpret the sign and magnitude.

children.title: Entity Resolution, Value Conflicts and Duplicates
children.body:
Entity Resolution

Entity resolution (record linkage) decides which records across sources describe the same entity. Exact matches on a key (passport number, GST number) are easy. Without a key, records are matched on combinations of name, address, date and other fields using similarity:

  • Exact match: "A56-A5" == "A56-A5".
  • String similarity: "IBM" vs "I.B.M." (edit distance, n-grams, phonetic codes like Soundex).
  • Numeric tolerance: two birth dates within a day are probably the same person.
  • Blocking: split candidates on city or surname first so fuzzy matching is not run over the whole dataset.

Detecting Duplicate Records

Duplicates inflate support counts and bias every model. Deduplication normally uses a canonical key, then removes rows with identical values across all fields, then reviews near-duplicates against a scoring threshold. Deduplication must be repeated after every integration, because joining tables creates new duplicates.

Value Conflicts

Even after entities are matched, the same attribute can disagree. Common conflict sources:

ConflictExampleResolution
UnitsSalary in INR vs USDConvert to one canonical unit
ScaleWeight in kg vs gNormalise to a standard scale
Encoding"Yes"/"No" vs 1/0 vs "Y"/"N"Map to one code set
Date formatDD/MM/YYYY vs YYYY-MM-DDParse to a single representation
Currency/regionCost incl. vs excl. taxRecord the convention in metadata
PrecisionHeight 1.8 vs 180 (cm vs m)Attach units to attributes

Three-Level Conflict Handling

  1. Schema level: make attribute definitions agree (same unit, same code set, same precision).
  2. Record level: make values from different sources fit the agreed schema (standardisation, mapping tables).
  3. Field level: when two sources genuinely disagree on a value, apply a rule: take the most recent, take the most trusted source, or keep both with a source tag.

Every conflict resolution should be recorded in metadata so it can be undone. A conflict that is silently resolved by "last write wins" is a common source of wrong results later in the pipeline.

Exam point: distinguish integration conflicts at the schema, record and field levels, and give two examples of value conflicts with their fixes.

children.title: Data Transformation Techniques
children.body:
What Transformation Does

Transformation changes the form or scale of values so that a mining algorithm can use them. Some algorithms require numeric input, some require nominal input, and distance-based algorithms require attributes to be on comparable scales. Transformation does not add information; it removes distortions that hide it.

Smoothing

Removes noise from an attribute. Binning, regression and clustering (covered under data cleaning) are the standard tools. Smoothing is often applied to time series before trend analysis.

Aggregation

Summarises data at a coarser granularity. Daily sales become monthly sales; per-store rows become per-city totals. Aggregation reduces the number of rows and typically produces more stable patterns, but it loses individual-level detail.

daily rows:   1,200  1,350  980  ...  -> monthly total: 38,400
per-store:    store A, B, C   -> per-city:   city X = A + B

Generalisation

Replaces low-level values by higher-level concepts. Age 17 becomes "teen", a street address becomes "city", a product SKU becomes "category". Generalisation maps naturally onto concept hierarchies and is useful when exact values are too detailed for the task.

Attribute Construction

Creates new attributes from existing ones. Examples: body mass index from height and weight; density from mass and volume; total spend from unit price and quantity; day-of-week from a date. Constructed attributes often expose patterns that no single original attribute contains.

Original attributesConstructed attributeWhy it helps
height, weightBMI = weight / height^2Encodes a meaningful ratio
unit price, quantitytotal = price x quantityCaptures transaction value
dateweekday, is_weekend, monthBrings cyclical patterns to the surface
systolic, diastolicpulse pressure = systolic - diastolicA clinical indicator

Normalisation

Rescales numeric values to a common range or distribution (min-max, z-score, decimal scaling). This is essential for distance-based methods such as k-NN, k-means and neural networks, because an attribute measured in lakhs otherwise dominates one measured in units.

Discretisation

Converts a continuous attribute into a small number of intervals: age into 0-18, 19-35, 36-60, 60+. This lets nominal algorithms use continuous data and can make patterns easier to interpret, at the cost of detail.

Exam point: list the six transformation techniques with one example each, and explain why normalisation is required before distance-based mining.

children.title: Normalization: Min-Max, Z-Score and Decimal Scaling
children.body:
Min-Max Normalisation

Maps every value linearly onto a target range, usually [0, 1]:

v' = (v - min) / (max - min)            target [0, 1]
v' = a + (v - min)(b - a) / (max - min) target [a, b]

It preserves the shape of the distribution and the order of values. It is sensitive to a single extreme value, because min and max are defined by the extremes.

Z-Score Normalisation (Zero-Mean)

Expresses each value as the number of standard deviations from the mean:

v' = (v - mean) / standard deviation

The result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It is robust to differences in scale and is the usual choice for attributes with a roughly normal distribution. Outliers still matter, because they influence the mean and standard deviation.

Decimal Scaling

Divides by a power of ten so that the largest absolute value is below 1:

v' = v / 10^j,  where j is the smallest integer such that max(|v'|) < 1

It is the simplest method and keeps the sign and relative spacing, but it does not equalise the ranges of different attributes.

Worked Example

Income values: 20,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000, 100,000. Mean = 60,000. Population standard deviation = 28,284.27.

IncomeMin-max [0,1]Min-max [10,20]Z-scoreDecimal scaling (j=5)
20,0000.00010.00-1.4140.2
40,0000.25012.50-0.7070.4
60,0000.50015.000.0000.6
80,0000.75017.500.7070.8
100,0001.00020.001.4141.0

Min-max check: (20,000 - 20,000) / 80,000 = 0; (40,000 - 20,000) / 80,000 = 0.25; and so on. Z-score check: (20,000 - 60,000) / 28,284.27 = -1.414.

children.title: Data Reduction: Overview and Data Cube Aggregation
children.body:
Why Reduce

A mining algorithm run on the full dataset may be too slow, may exceed memory, or may overfit to noise in thousands of attributes. Data reduction produces a smaller representation that yields almost the same mining result. The reduced dataset should be much smaller, yet the patterns found on it should be close to the patterns in the original.

Three Families of Reduction

  • Dimensionality reduction: fewer attributes (attribute subset selection, PCA, wavelet transforms).
  • Numerosity reduction: fewer rows (histograms, clustering, sampling, regression models).
  • Data compression: smaller encoding of the same data (lossless such as gzip, lossy such as wavelets or PCA).

Reduction can be lossless (the original can be reconstructed exactly, as with a lossless compression or removing a duplicate column) or lossy (information is discarded, as with sampling or dropping low-variance attributes). Lossy reduction is acceptable when the lost detail does not change the mining result.

Data Cube Aggregation

When data is stored in a data warehouse, aggregation is the cheapest reduction. Sales recorded per day can be summed to quarters or years; a data cube can be rolled up along any dimension. The cube is smaller and the mining question ("which region grew fastest this year?") is directly answered by the aggregated cells.

sales(day, store, product)          full cube: many cells
  roll up day -> quarter          4x fewer time cells
  roll up store -> city            fewer location cells
  roll up product -> category      fewer product cells
result: aggregated cube, same totals, far fewer rows

Aggregation is lossless with respect to the totals but lossy with respect to individual records. If a pattern depends on individual transactions (for example, market-basket rules), aggregation destroys it, so the reduction must match the mining goal.

Exam point: name the three families, classify each technique as lossless or lossy, and explain data cube aggregation with a roll-up example.

children.title: Attribute Subset Selection
children.body:
The Idea

Many datasets contain attributes that are irrelevant or redundant. Attribute subset selection keeps a small subset that preserves the class distribution. Removing noise attributes usually improves accuracy as well as speed, because algorithms stop fitting spurious correlations.

Heuristic Search

Testing every subset is exponential, so practical methods use greedy search with an evaluation measure:

  1. Stepwise forward selection: start with an empty set; repeatedly add the attribute that most improves the measure; stop when no attribute improves it.
  2. Stepwise backward elimination: start with all attributes; repeatedly remove the attribute whose removal hurts least; stop when removal hurts too much.
  3. Combination: forward selection followed by backward checks, which catches attributes that only help in combination.

Evaluation Measures

  • Information gain: pick attributes that reduce class entropy the most (the same measure used by ID3 decision trees).
  • Gini index: pick attributes that most reduce class impurity (used by CART).
  • Statistical significance: keep attributes whose association with the class is significant (chi-square, t-test).
  • Wrapper accuracy: train the actual mining algorithm on each candidate subset and keep the subset with the best cross-validated accuracy. Accurate but expensive.

Decision-Tree Induction as a Filter

A fast and popular heuristic is to build a decision tree on all attributes and keep only the attributes that appear in the tree. Attributes never chosen by the tree are treated as irrelevant. This is a filter: it is fast, but the selection is biased toward attributes that suit trees.

all attributes ---- build decision tree ---- keep attributes used in splits
     |                                              |
     +------> repeated on the reduced set until no gain <------+

Worked Mini Example

Predict whether a customer buys a product from four attributes: age, income, city, has_children. Stepwise forward selection with information gain might add income first (largest gain), then age (next largest gain given income), then stop when city and has_children add nothing. The reduced dataset uses two attributes instead of four and loses no measurable accuracy.

Filter, Wrapper and Embedded

TypeHow it selectsCost
FilterRank attributes by a statistical score, independent of the algorithmLow
WrapperSearch subsets and evaluate with the mining algorithmHigh, but tailored
EmbeddedSelection happens while the model is trained (e.g. tree splits, L1 penalty)Medium

Exam point: describe forward selection and backward elimination step by step, then explain why decision-tree induction is a useful heuristic filter.

children.title: Dimensionality Reduction: PCA and Wavelets
children.body:
The Curse of Dimensionality

As the number of attributes grows, data becomes sparse: distance measures lose contrast, and the number of samples needed for a reliable model grows exponentially. Dimensionality reduction projects or transforms the data into fewer dimensions while keeping most of the structure.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA finds new axes (principal components) that are linear combinations of the original attributes and are ordered by how much variance they explain. The first component points in the direction of greatest variance, the second is orthogonal to it and explains the next greatest variance, and so on. Keeping the first k components gives a lower-dimensional representation with minimal squared reconstruction error.

  1. Centre the data: subtract the mean of each attribute.
  2. Compute the covariance matrix of the centred data.
  3. Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Each eigenvector is a principal component; its eigenvalue is the variance explained.
  4. Sort components by eigenvalue, keep the top k, and project each record onto them.
  5. Choose k from the cumulative explained variance, for example keep components until 95 percent is reached.

A Small Worked Case

Four points: (2,3), (3,4), (4,5), (5,6). Every point lies on the line y = x + 1, so the data is really one-dimensional. The covariance matrix has one non-zero eigenvalue (2.5) and one zero eigenvalue (0). The first component (1, 1)/sqrt(2) explains 100 percent of the variance; projecting onto it reduces two attributes to one with no loss.

y ^
  |       o
  |     o
  |   o
  | o
  +-----------> x
all points on a line: one principal component is enough

For real data the variance is spread over several components. Keeping the first two of twenty explains perhaps 90 percent, so 20 attributes become 2 and the mining algorithm runs far faster. PCA is unsupervised: it ignores the class label, so a component that separates classes but has low variance can be lost.

Wavelet Transform

A wavelet transform replaces the data by a sum of scaled and shifted wavelets, concentrating information into a few large coefficients. It is often used for images, signals and time series. The simplest example is the Haar transform, which repeatedly replaces pairs (a, b) by an average and a difference:

values       4    6    8   10
level 1: (4+6)/2=5  (8+10)/2=9   differences: 4-6=-2, 8-10=-2
level 2: (5+9)/2=7               difference: 5-9=-4
result: 7, -4, -2, -2   (one large average, small details)

Dropping the small detail coefficients keeps the broad shape while reducing the number of values. Unlike PCA, wavelets preserve locality, so a spike at one time or place stays localised instead of being spread across all components.

MethodKeepsBest for
PCAGlobal variance, orthogonal componentsWide numeric tables, compression before clustering
WaveletsLocal structure at multiple scalesImages, signals, time series

Exam point: list the PCA steps, explain that eigenvectors give directions and eigenvalues give explained variance, and describe the Haar wavelet transform with a small example.

children.title: Numerosity Reduction: Histograms, Sampling and Clustering
children.body:
Reducing the Number of Rows

Numerosity reduction replaces the original rows with a smaller model of them. The two families are parametric (store a model such as a regression, not the data) and non-parametric (store a summary such as a histogram, a cluster of representatives or a sample).

Histograms

A histogram partitions values into buckets and stores the count or sum per bucket. It is a compact summary of one attribute, and several attributes can be summarised by a multidimensional histogram.

  • Equal-width: the range is divided into k equal intervals. Simple, but skewed data puts most points in one bucket.
  • Equal-frequency (equi-depth): each bucket holds roughly the same number of points. Handles skew better, but boundaries depend on the data.
  • V-optimal: chooses bucket boundaries to minimise the variance within buckets, giving the best approximation for a given number of buckets.

Example: ages 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 31, 33, 35, 60 with three equal-frequency buckets gives about three ages each; three equal-width buckets over 20 to 60 gives 20-33, 33-46, 46-60, and the last bucket holds only the value 60.

Sampling

Sampling is the most common reduction for very large data. A sample is much cheaper to mine, and with a large enough sample the pattern found is close to the pattern in the full data.

MethodHow it worksNote
Simple random sampling without replacement (SRSWOR)Pick n of N rows, each subset equally likelyMost common
Simple random sampling with replacement (SRSWR)Pick n rows one at a time, allowing repeatsTheoretical convenience
Stratified samplingSample within each class or group, then combineKeeps rare classes represented
Cluster samplingPick whole groups (clusters) at randomCheap when data is physically grouped
Adaptive samplingIncrease the sample when the estimate is unstableUseful for approximate query answers

A sample of size n estimates a proportion p with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n). For p = 0.5 and n = 1,000 the standard error is about 1.6 percent, which is why 1,000 to 10,000 rows often suffice even when the dataset has millions. Sampling must be random: taking the first n rows biases the result toward whatever order the data was stored in.

Clustering and Regression

Clustering can reduce rows by replacing each cluster with its centre or medoid. Regression reduces a numeric attribute to a model y = a + bx (or a multiple regression), storing the coefficients instead of every point. Both are lossy: clustering loses individual variation, and regression loses everything that the model does not explain.

Choosing a Reduction

SituationReasonable choice
Very large row count, pattern is globalRandom or stratified sample
Need a quick profile of one attributeHistogram
Many correlated numeric attributesPCA
Data is physically clustered by region or timeCluster sampling
Need row-level representativesClustering with centroids

Exam point: compare SRSWOR, SRSWR, stratified and cluster sampling, and be ready to histogram a small list of values by equal width and equal frequency.

children.title: Discretization Methods
children.body:
Why Discretize

Discretisation replaces a continuous attribute by a small number of intervals (also called bins or buckets). It lets algorithms that only accept nominal attributes (classic ID3, association rule mining) use numeric data, reduces the effect of noise and makes rules easier to read: "age 19-35" is clearer than "age < 35.5 and age > 18.5".

A discretisation method is described by three choices: how many intervals, where the boundaries go, and whether the class label is used.

Unsupervised Methods

  • Equal-width binning: divide [min, max] into k intervals of equal width. Simple, but a skewed attribute puts almost every value in one bin.
  • Equal-frequency binning: choose boundaries so each interval holds about the same number of values. Better for skew, but identical values may have to be split.
  • Histogram analysis: use the buckets of a histogram as intervals, optionally merging adjacent buckets with similar counts.
  • Cluster analysis: run k-means on the attribute and use the clusters as intervals. Adapts to the data distribution.

Supervised Methods

Supervised methods use the class label to place boundaries where they separate classes best.

  • Entropy-based (information gain): choose the split that reduces class entropy the most, then recurse. This is the discretisation used inside decision-tree induction.
  • Chi-merge: start with one interval per distinct value, then repeatedly merge the adjacent pair with the smallest chi-square value until a stopping rule is met.
  • Bayesian and cluster-based supervised methods: model the class distribution inside each interval and merge intervals that are statistically similar.

Entropy-Based Split: Worked Example

Eight ordered values with class labels. Total entropy of the class distribution:

labels:   N  N  Y  N  Y  Y  Y  Y
counts:   N = 3, Y = 5

H(D) = -(3/8)log2(3/8) - (5/8)log2(5/8)
     = 0.5306 + 0.4238 = 0.9544

Try boundaries after the 2nd, 4th and 6th values:

BoundaryLeft intervalRight intervalWeighted entropyInformation gain
after 2N, N (entropy 0)Y, N, Y, Y, Y, Y (1N, 5Y, 0.6500)(2/8)x0 + (6/8)x0.6500 = 0.48750.4669
after 4N, N, Y, N (3N, 1Y, 0.8113)Y, Y, Y, Y (entropy 0)(4/8)x0.8113 + (4/8)x0 = 0.40560.5488
after 6N, N, Y, N, Y, Y (3N, 3Y, 1.0000)Y, Y (entropy 0)(6/8)x1.0000 + (2/8)x0 = 0.75000.2044

The split after the 4th value has the highest gain (0.5488), so the first boundary is placed there. The left interval is still impure (3 N, 1 Y), so the same procedure recurses inside it. Recursion stops when an interval is pure, holds too few values, or no split gives a positive gain.

Chi-Merge: Worked Idea

For two adjacent intervals with class counts, build a 2 x c contingency table and compute chi-square. The pair with the smallest value is the most similar and is merged first. Merging repeats until the smallest chi-square exceeds a threshold or the number of intervals reaches the target.

Comparison

MethodUses class?StrengthWeakness
Equal widthNoTrivial, interpretableBad with skew or outliers
Equal frequencyNoBalanced binsSplits equal values, ignores class
Cluster basedNoAdapts to distributionNeeds k, unstable
Entropy basedYesClass-aware, good for treesCan overfit with many intervals
Chi-mergeYesStatistically principledSensitive to threshold

Exam point: discretise a short labelled list by equal width, equal frequency and entropy gain. Show the entropy values; examiners look for H(D) = -sum p log2 p and the weighted entropy calculation.

children.title: Concept Hierarchy Generation
children.body:
What a Concept Hierarchy Is

A concept hierarchy organises values from specific to general: street, city, district, state, country; or product SKU, subcategory, category, department. Mining at a higher level gives compact, general rules; drilling down gives detail. Hierarchies are the basis of roll-up and drill-down in OLAP and of multi-level association rules.

country
  |
state
  |
district
  |
city
  |
street

Schema-Level Generation

Some hierarchies follow directly from the schema. If the attributes street, city, state and country are all present, their order is obvious and can be declared in the data dictionary. Partial orders are also common: street is below city, but a product hierarchy and a location hierarchy are independent.

Data-Driven Generation

When only the raw values are available, the hierarchy is derived from the data. For a location attribute, collect the distinct values and count how often each one occurs. Values that occur many times are likely to be high-level concepts; values that occur once are likely to be leaves.

ValueDistinct valuesCoverageInterpretation
country15100%Top level
province/state365100%Second level
city3,567~99%Third level
street674,339~99%Leaf level

A useful heuristic: if a field has only a few distinct values and covers all records, it is a general concept; if it has very many distinct values, it is a leaf. The first few fields ordered by increasing distinct count form the hierarchy. Missing coverage tells you where values do not follow the hierarchy and need manual review.

Automatic Hierarchy Generation

For a set of values such as city names, the hierarchy can be generated automatically by grouping values that share tokens or by using reference data (postal code prefixes, administrative boundaries). The result is a tree whose depth is chosen by the analyst, not by the data alone.

Using Hierarchies in Mining

  • Multi-level association rules: "bread to milk" can be generalised to "bakery to dairy".
  • Roll-up and drill-down in a data cube.
  • Generalisation in data transformation: replace a street by its city.
  • Reducing cardinality: a high-cardinality attribute such as city becomes a small set of regions.

Exam point: explain schema-level versus data-driven hierarchy generation, and be able to derive a location hierarchy from a table of distinct value counts.

children.title: Preprocessing Pipeline and Common Pitfalls
children.body:
A Reliable Order of Work

  1. Profile the data: counts, missing percentages, ranges, distinct values, duplicates.
  2. Split into training and test sets before any fitting step.
  3. Clean: fix types, standardise formats, handle missing values, remove duplicates.
  4. Integrate: join sources, resolve entities and conflicts.
  5. Construct and transform attributes, then fit normalisation on the training set only.
  6. Reduce and discretise if the algorithm or dataset needs it.
  7. Re-apply the fitted transformations to the test set, and store them for production.

Data Leakage

Leakage is the most damaging preprocessing mistake: information from the test set reaches the model during training. The model looks excellent in evaluation and fails in production.

  • Fitting min-max, z-score or PCA on the full dataset leaks the test distribution. Fit on training data, transform the test data with the saved parameters.
  • Imputing missing values with a statistic computed from all rows leaks test values.
  • Deduplicating after the split can leave the same entity in both sets. Deduplicate before splitting.
  • Oversampling a class before splitting duplicates minority rows into the test set. Split first, then resample the training fold.

Class Imbalance and Sampling Bias

A dataset with 99 percent negatives makes accuracy misleading. Keep enough positives in the test set, use stratified splitting, and report precision, recall and F1 rather than accuracy. Random sampling of rows can wipe out a rare class entirely; stratified sampling keeps it.

Time and Order

For time-series or event data, do not split randomly. Train on the past and test on the future. Random preprocessing such as shuffling or random sampling can break the temporal order and create rules that cannot be used in production.

Reproducibility

  • Record every transformation, its parameters and the code that applied it.
  • Set random seeds for sampling, clustering and neural network initialisation.
  • Keep the raw data immutable; write cleaned data to a new file or table.
  • Re-run the pipeline end to end when the source data changes, instead of patching results.

Checklist

CheckWhy it matters
Missing-value rate per columnHigh-missingness columns may be useless or need a different method
Duplicate rateInflates support and accuracy
Outlier counts after cappingConfirms the rule did what you expected
Class balance before and after samplingAvoids a silently biased training set
Scaler fitted on train onlyPrevents leakage
Transformations saved with the modelMakes production scoring possible

Exam point: leakage and the train/test split are frequent short-answer questions. Say clearly which statistics may be computed from training data only.

children.title: Important Definitions and Quick Revision
children.body:
Important Definitions

  • Data preprocessing: the set of techniques that clean, integrate, transform and reduce raw data before mining.
  • Data cleaning: filling missing values, smoothing noise, removing outliers and resolving inconsistencies.
  • Data integration: combining data from multiple sources into one coherent store.
  • Entity resolution: deciding which records from different sources describe the same real-world object.
  • Data transformation: changing the form or scale of values (smoothing, aggregation, generalisation, attribute construction, normalisation, discretisation).
  • Data reduction: producing a smaller representation that gives almost the same mining result.
  • Dimensionality reduction: reducing the number of attributes (attribute subset selection, PCA, wavelets).
  • Numerosity reduction: reducing the number of rows (histograms, sampling, clustering, regression).
  • Normalisation: rescaling numeric values to a common range or distribution.
  • Min-max normalisation: v' = (v - min) / (max - min).
  • Z-score normalisation: v' = (v - mean) / standard deviation.
  • Discretisation: replacing a continuous attribute by a small number of intervals.
  • Concept hierarchy: an ordering of values from specific to general, such as street to country.
  • Binning: sorting values and smoothing each group by its mean, median or boundaries.
  • Chi-square test: tests whether two categorical attributes are dependent by comparing observed and expected counts.
  • PCA: a linear projection onto orthogonal components ordered by explained variance.
  • Sampling: selecting a representative subset of rows, with or without replacement, stratified or clustered.

Important Formulas

min-max:    v' = (v - min) / (max - min)
z-score:    v' = (v - mean) / sd
decimal:    v' = v / 10^j
entropy:    H(D) = -sum p_i log2 p_i
info gain:  Gain(A) = H(D) - sum (|Dj|/|D|) H(Dj)
chi-square: X^2 = sum (O - E)^2 / E
covariance: cov(A,B) = sum (Ai - meanA)(Bi - meanB) / n
correlation: corr(A,B) = cov(A,B) / (sdA sdB)
standard error of a proportion: sqrt(p(1-p)/n)

Important Comparisons

  1. Data cleaning vs data integration vs data transformation vs data reduction.
  2. MCAR vs MAR vs MNAR.
  3. Dropping missing rows vs mean imputation vs predictive imputation.
  4. Equal-width vs equal-frequency binning.
  5. Min-max vs z-score vs decimal scaling normalisation.
  6. PCA vs wavelet transform.
  7. Simple random vs stratified vs cluster sampling.
  8. Entropy-based discretisation vs equal-width binning.
  9. Schema-level vs data-driven concept hierarchy generation.
  10. Lossless vs lossy reduction.

Important Diagrams to Practise

  1. The preprocessing pipeline: cleaning, integration, transformation, reduction, discretisation.
  2. The five tasks mapped onto the KDD process.
  3. Sorting values into bins and smoothing by mean, median and boundaries.
  4. A regression line or curve smoothing noisy points.
  5. A PCA projection from two dimensions to one principal component.
  6. A histogram with equal-width and equal-frequency buckets.
  7. An entropy-based split tree on a small labelled dataset.
  8. A concept hierarchy from street to country.

Important Long-Answer Questions

  1. Explain why data preprocessing is needed and describe its five major tasks.
  2. Explain the different mechanisms of missing data and the methods used to handle them.
  3. Explain noise, binning, regression and clustering as data cleaning techniques with examples.
  4. Explain data integration, entity identification and redundancy analysis.
  5. Compute chi-square and covariance for a small example and interpret the results.
  6. Explain the data transformation techniques with examples.
  7. Explain min-max, z-score and decimal-scaling normalisation with a worked example.
  8. Explain attribute subset selection with forward selection and backward elimination.
  9. Explain PCA step by step and describe the wavelet transform.
  10. Explain histograms, sampling methods and clustering as numerosity reduction.
  11. Explain discretisation by binning, entropy and chi-merge with examples.
  12. Explain concept hierarchy generation at the schema level and from data.

Important Short-Answer Questions

  1. Define data preprocessing.
  2. List the four characteristics of data quality.
  3. What is noisy data?
  4. What is an outlier?
  5. Define data integration.
  6. What is entity identification?
  7. What does a chi-square test measure?
  8. What is redundancy?

  11. When is z-score normalisation preferred?
  12. What is decimal scaling?
  13. Define data reduction.
  14. What is dimensionality reduction?

  16. What is PCA?
  17. What is a wavelet transform?
  18. Define sampling and name two methods.
  19. What is discretisation?

Study Strategy

  • Learn the five tasks and the problem each solves; most long answers start there.
  • Practise the three normalisation formulas on a list of five numbers until they are automatic.
  • Practise one full entropy-based split; the arithmetic is where marks are lost.
  • Draw the binning example by hand and check the bin mean, median and boundary results.
  • Remember that PCA components are ordered by eigenvalue, and that eigenvalues measure explained variance.
  • For sampling, remember that stratified sampling protects rare classes and cluster sampling is cheaper but less precise.
  • Link every technique to a mining algorithm that needs it: normalisation for k-NN and k-means, discretisation for ID3 and association rules, reduction for scalability.
  • Revise the pitfalls: leakage, imputing before splitting and deduplicating after splitting.

Important: Module 2 questions are usually numerical. A correct formula with a small worked example is worth more than a long definition. Always state the assumption behind a method (MCAR for simple imputation, linearity for regression, independence for chi-square).

children.title: Classification: Concepts and Two-Step Process
children.body:
What Classification Is

Classification is a supervised learning task: given a set of records whose class label is known, build a model that assigns a class label to new, unseen records. The label is categorical (spam or not spam, safe or risky, pass or fail). When the target is continuous the task is called prediction or regression.

Classification is used for credit approval, fraud detection, medical diagnosis, churn prediction, image recognition and document categorisation. It is the most widely used data mining function.

The Two-Step Process

  1. Learning (training) step: a classification algorithm learns a model from a training set of labelled records. The model can be a decision tree, a set of rules, a neural network, a Bayesian model or a distance-based classifier.
  2. Classification (testing) step: the model is used to predict labels for new records. Its accuracy is estimated on a test set whose labels were held back, not on the training data.
labelled data ---> learning algorithm ---> model
                                              |
new, unlabelled records ---> model ---> predicted labels
                                              |
                         compare with known labels on a test set
                                              |
                                      accuracy estimate

Training and Test Data

The labelled dataset is split into a training set (typically 60 to 80 percent) and a test set (the rest). The split must be random but stratified, so each class is represented in both parts. For time-dependent data the split is chronological: train on the past, test on the future.

Evaluating on the training set is a mistake: a model that simply memorises the training records scores 100 percent and is useless on new data. This is overfitting.

Issues in Classification

  • Data preparation: missing values, noise and unscaled attributes must be handled first.
  • Model choice: different algorithms fit different shapes of decision boundary; no single algorithm is best for every dataset.
  • Overfitting and underfitting: too complex a model fits noise; too simple a model misses the pattern.
  • Class imbalance: a rare class is easily ignored by an accuracy-driven model.
  • Cost of errors: a false negative in cancer screening is far worse than a false positive, so the evaluation must reflect costs.
  • Interpretability: a decision tree is readable; a deep neural network is not, which matters in medicine and law.

A Simple Example

A bank wants to classify loan applicants as "safe" or "risky". Historical records contain income, existing debt, employment years and whether the loan was repaid. The learning step builds a model such as: "if debt-to-income ratio is above 0.5 and employment is under one year, predict risky". The testing step applies the rule to new applicants and counts how often it agrees with the actual outcome.

Exam point: define classification, draw the two-step diagram and explain why the test set must be separate from the training set.

children.title: Classification vs Prediction vs Clustering
children.body:
Three Different Tasks

AspectClassificationPrediction (regression)Clustering
SupervisionSupervisedSupervisedUnsupervised
TargetCategorical class labelContinuous numeric valueNo label; groups are discovered
Training dataLabelled recordsLabelled records with numeric targetUnlabelled records
Typical algorithmsDecision tree, naive Bayes, k-NN, SVM, neural networkLinear regression, regression tree, neural networkk-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN
OutputA class, a rule set, a treeA numeric estimateClusters and cluster descriptions
ExampleWill this customer churn?How much will this customer spend?Which customer segments exist?

Why the Distinction Matters

Supervised methods can be evaluated against known answers, so accuracy, precision, recall and error are directly measurable. Clustering has no ground truth: quality is judged by internal measures (compactness, separation) or by how useful the clusters turn out to be. Applying classification metrics to clustering is a common conceptual error.

Classification and Prediction Together

Many real problems combine the two. A churn model first classifies whether a customer will leave and then predicts how much revenue would be lost. A hospital model classifies a patient as high risk and predicts the expected length of stay. The classification part often uses a discrete threshold on a predicted probability, which shows how closely the tasks are related.

Methods That Do Both

  • Regression trees and model trees produce both a class (by leaf majority) and a numeric estimate (by leaf average).
  • Neural networks can have several outputs: a categorical label plus a numeric score.
  • k-NN can classify (majority vote) or predict (average of neighbours).
  • Naive Bayes naturally outputs a probability, which can be thresholded into a class.

Exam point: a three-column comparison of classification, prediction and clustering is a standard short-answer question. Mention supervision, target type and an example for each.

children.title: Decision Trees: Principle and Tree Construction
children.body:
What a Decision Tree Is

A decision tree is a flowchart-like structure. Each internal node tests one attribute, each branch is one outcome of the test, and each leaf carries a class label (or a predicted value). A record is classified by starting at the root and following the branches according to its attribute values until a leaf is reached.

              outlook
              /  |  \
          sunny  overcast  rain
            /        |        \
        humidity   play=Yes    wind
          /  \                  /  \
       high  normal        strong  weak
        /      \            /        \
      No      Yes         No        Yes

The tree above says: if outlook is overcast, play; if sunny, play only when humidity is normal; if rain, play only when wind is weak.

The General Algorithm

Most tree induction algorithms follow the same recursive "divide and conquer" scheme (this is the essence of ID3):

  1. If all records in the node have the same class, make the node a leaf with that class.
  2. If no attributes remain, make the node a leaf with the majority class.
  3. Otherwise choose the "best" attribute using an attribute selection measure, and split the node into branches, one per value of that attribute.
  4. Recurse on each branch with the remaining attributes.

Attribute Selection Measures

The heart of the algorithm is choosing which attribute to test at each node. The chosen attribute should separate the classes as cleanly as possible. Three measures are taught:

  • Information gain (ID3): pick the attribute that most reduces class entropy.
  • Gain ratio (C4.5): normalise information gain against the number of branches, so attributes with many values are not over-praised.
  • Gini index (CART): pick the attribute that most reduces impurity, using the Gini coefficient.

Stopping Rules

  • The node is pure: all records share one class.
  • No attributes are left to test.
  • The node holds fewer records than a minimum threshold, to avoid overfitting tiny subproblems.
  • No attribute gives a significant improvement, so the node becomes a leaf by majority vote.

Strengths and Weaknesses

  • Trees are fast to build and use, easy to interpret and can handle both numeric and nominal attributes.
  • Small trees generalise well, but deep unpruned trees overfit.
  • Trees are sensitive to small changes in the training data; a different sample can produce a very different tree.
  • Classic trees only split on one attribute at a time, so diagonal decision boundaries need many splits (or a different model).

Exam point: describe the recursive tree-construction algorithm and draw a small tree from a given dataset. Be ready to show the attribute selection calculations in the next notes.

children.title: Attribute Selection: Information Gain and Entropy
children.body:
Entropy

Entropy measures the impurity, or uncertainty, of a set of records. For a set S with classes c1 to ck, with pi the fraction of records in class ci:

H(S) = - p1 log2 p1 - p2 log2 p2 - ... - pk log2 pk

p = 1 or 0  ->  H = 0            (perfectly pure)
p = 0.5, 0.5 ->  H = 1            (maximum uncertainty)
for k classes the maximum is log2 k

Information Gain

After splitting on attribute A with v values, the weighted average entropy of the branches is subtracted from the entropy before the split:

Gain(A) = H(S) - sum over values v of ( |Sv| / |S| ) H(Sv)

where Sv is the subset of S with value v of attribute A.

The attribute with the highest gain is chosen; it removes the most uncertainty.

Worked Example: The Play Dataset

Fourteen days described by outlook, temperature, humidity and wind; the label says whether play happened. There are 9 Yes and 5 No:

H(S) = -(9/14) log2(9/14) - (5/14) log2(5/14)
     = 0.4098 + 0.5305 = 0.940

Information gain for each attribute:

temperaturehot 4 (2,2), mild 6 (4,2), cool 4 (3,1)1, 0.918, 0.811(4/14)1 + (6/14)0.918 + (4/14)0.811 = 0.9110.029
humidityhigh 7 (3,4), normal 7 (6,1)0.985, 0.592(7/14)0.985 + (7/14)0.592 = 0.7890.151
windweak 8 (6,2), strong 6 (3,3)0.811, 1(8/14)0.811 + (6/14)1 = 0.8920.048

Outlook has the largest gain, so the root tests outlook.

Recursing on the Sunny Branch

The five sunny records have 2 Yes and 3 No, so H = -(2/5)log2(2/5) - (3/5)log2(3/5) = 0.971. Gains inside this subset:

AttributeGain
humidity1.000 (high 3,0 splits it perfectly)
