wind0.020

Humidity is chosen: high means No, normal means Yes. The rain branch (3 Yes, 2 No) splits perfectly on wind: weak means Yes, strong means No. Overcast is already pure Yes. The tree is complete.

Gain Ratio (C4.5)

Information gain favours attributes with many values: an ID column splits every record into its own branch and scores the maximum gain. The gain ratio divides the gain by the split information, which grows with the number and evenness of branches, penalising wide splits:

SplitInfo(A) = - sum ( |Sv| / |S| ) log2 ( |Sv| / |S| )
GainRatio(A) = Gain(A) / SplitInfo(A)

Exam point: compute H(S), the weighted entropy and the gain for a small dataset, then pick the best attribute. Always show the entropy arithmetic; that is where the marks are.

children.title: Attribute Selection: Gini Index
children.body:
Gini Impurity

The Gini index measures how often a randomly chosen record would be labelled incorrectly if labels were assigned according to the class distribution in the node. For a node with classes c1 to ck and fractions pi:

Gini(S) = 1 - sum ( pi^2 )

pure node: 1 - 1^2 = 0
50/50 two classes: 1 - 0.25 - 0.25 = 0.5

For a split on attribute A, the Gini index of the split is the weighted average of the child Gini values. The attribute with the smallest weighted Gini (equivalently, the largest reduction) is chosen. CART uses binary splits: every attribute value is tested against the rest, and the best binary partition is kept.

Worked Example: The Same Play Dataset

Gini(S) = 1 - (9/14)^2 - (5/14)^2 = 1 - 0.4133 - 0.1276 = 0.4592
AttributeChild Gini valuesWeighted GiniReduction
outlooksunny 1-(2/5)^2-(3/5)^2 = 0.480; overcast 0; rain 0.480(5/14)0.480 + 0 + (5/14)0.480 = 0.3430.116
temperaturehot 0.500; mild 0.444; cool 0.375(4/14)0.500 + (6/14)0.444 + (4/14)0.375 = 0.4410.018
humidityhigh 0.490; normal 0.245(7/14)0.490 + (7/14)0.245 = 0.3670.092
windweak 0.375; strong 0.500(8/14)0.375 + (6/14)0.500 = 0.4290.031

Outlook again has the smallest weighted Gini (largest reduction), so it is chosen as the root. On this dataset Gini and information gain agree; on others they can choose different attributes.

Gini for a Binary Split

CART does not create one branch per value. For a numeric attribute it sorts the values and tries every midpoint; for a nominal attribute it tries every subset against its complement. Each candidate produces two children, and the split with the lowest weighted Gini wins. This keeps trees binary and makes the arithmetic slightly different from ID3.

Entropy vs Gini

AspectInformation gain (entropy)Gini index
Formula-sum p log2 p1 - sum p^2
Typical algorithmID3, C4.5CART, random forests
CostLogarithm per classMultiplication only (faster)
BehaviourSlightly more sensitive to small changesSlightly more balanced splits
Multi-way splitsNaturalUsually binary

Exam point: be able to compute both measures for the same attribute and explain why they sometimes disagree. Remember that the chosen attribute has the highest gain but the lowest Gini.

children.title: ID3, C4.5 and CART; Overfitting and Pruning
children.body:
The Three Classic Algorithms

FeatureID3C4.5CART
Split criterionInformation gainGain ratioGini index
Split shapeMulti-way, one branch per valueMulti-way, can group valuesBinary
Numeric attributesRequires discretisationHandles thresholds directlyHandles thresholds directly
Missing valuesNot handled wellHandled by fractional weightsHandled by surrogate splits
PruningNone built inPessimistic error pruningCost-complexity pruning
OutputTreeTree or rule setTree (classification or regression)

Why Trees Overfit

If the tree is grown until every leaf is pure, it starts to memorise noise: a leaf with a single training record has 100 percent training accuracy and no predictive value. Deep trees also encode spurious splits on attributes that happen to separate a handful of records.

The classic symptom is a large gap between training accuracy (near 100 percent) and test accuracy (much lower). The cure is pruning: remove branches that do not improve generalisation.

Pre-Pruning

Stop growing before the tree is complete. A node is not split if the split does not improve a statistical measure by a minimum amount, if the node has fewer than a minimum number of records, or if the resulting depth exceeds a limit. Pre-pruning is fast, but it can stop too early: a split that looks weak now may enable a strong split below it (the "horizon effect").

Post-Pruning

Grow the full tree, then remove subtrees that do not pay for themselves. The two standard methods:

  • Pessimistic error pruning (C4.5): estimate the error of each subtree on the training data with a pessimistic correction, and replace a subtree by a leaf when the leaf is estimated to be at least as accurate.
  • Cost-complexity pruning (CART): choose a sequence of pruned trees that trades training error against tree size, and select the best one by cross-validation.
full tree:   deep, training error 0.00, test error 0.22
after prune:shallower, training error 0.06, test error 0.14

pruning accepts a small training loss to reduce test error

Other Ways to Control Tree Size

  • Limit maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf and minimum samples per split.
  • Require a minimum gain or minimum Gini reduction for a split.
  • Use an ensemble: bagged trees (random forests) average many trees and are far more stable than one tree.
  • Cross-validate the pruning parameter instead of choosing it by intuition.

Exam point: compare ID3, C4.5 and CART in a table, then explain pre-pruning versus post-pruning with one advantage and one disadvantage each.

children.title: Naive Bayes Classification
children.body:
Bayes Theorem

Bayesian classification uses Bayes theorem to estimate the probability of each class given the observed attribute values, and predicts the class with the highest probability:

P(C | X) = P(X | C) * P(C) / P(X)

P(C)      prior probability of class C
P(X | C)  likelihood of the attribute values in class C
P(X)      evidence, the same for every class

Because P(X) is constant across classes, comparison only needs P(X | C) P(C). The predicted class is the one that maximises this product.

The Naive Assumption

Computing P(X | C) for a full combination of attributes needs an enormous number of records. Naive Bayes assumes that attributes are conditionally independent given the class, so the likelihood factorises:

P(X | C) = P(x1 | C) * P(x2 | C) * ... * P(xn | C)

This assumption is almost never exactly true (attributes are usually correlated), yet the classifier works well in practice, especially for text and high-dimensional data. It is called "naive" because of this simplification.

Worked Example

Using the play dataset (9 Yes, 5 No), classify X = (outlook = sunny, temperature = cool, humidity = high, wind = strong).

TermClass YesClass No
P(C)9/14 = 0.6435/14 = 0.357
P(sunny | C)2/9 = 0.2223/5 = 0.600
P(cool | C)3/9 = 0.3331/5 = 0.200
P(high | C)3/9 = 0.3334/5 = 0.800
P(strong | C)3/9 = 0.3333/5 = 0.600
Product P(X|C) P(C)0.00530.0206
Yes: 0.222 * 0.333 * 0.333 * 0.333 * 0.643 = 0.0053
No:  0.600 * 0.200 * 0.800 * 0.600 * 0.357 = 0.0206

normalise: 0.0053 / 0.0259 = 0.20   and   0.0206 / 0.0259 = 0.80
prediction: No (80 percent confidence)

Zero-Frequency Problem and Smoothing

If a value never appears with a class in the training data, its conditional probability is 0 and the whole product becomes 0 regardless of the other evidence. Laplace smoothing adds a small count to every value:

P(xi | C) = ( count(xi, C) + 1 ) / ( count(C) + number_of_values(xi) )

A general m-estimate uses a weight m and a prior p: (count + m p) / (count(C) + m). Smoothing keeps the classifier usable when a rare combination is missing from the training sample.

Strengths and Weaknesses

  • Very fast to train and to predict; training is just counting.
  • Handles many attributes and high-dimensional data (text) well.
  • Gives a probability estimate, which is useful for ranking and for cost-sensitive decisions.
  • Cannot model interactions between attributes: the independence assumption limits accuracy when attributes are strongly correlated.
  • The probability estimates are often over-confident (too close to 0 or 1) even when the predicted class is correct.

Exam point: state Bayes theorem, list the independence assumption, and perform the full worked calculation. Mention Laplace smoothing if any conditional probability is zero.

children.title: k-Nearest Neighbours (k-NN)
children.body:
The Idea

k-Nearest Neighbours is an instance-based (lazy) classifier: it stores the training data and does no work until a prediction is requested. For a new record, it finds the k closest training records and assigns the majority class among them (or averages their values for prediction).

Algorithm

  1. Choose k, the number of neighbours.
  2. Compute the distance from the new record to every training record.
  3. Select the k records with the smallest distances.
  4. Classify by majority vote (or by a distance-weighted vote). Break ties by summing the distances or by choosing the class of the closest neighbour.
query q ---> distances to all training records ---> sort ---> take k
                                                              |
                                        majority vote / weighted vote
                                                              |
                                                          predicted class

Distance Measures

Euclidean distance is usual for continuous attributes; Manhattan distance is more robust to outliers; Hamming distance is used for binary or categorical values; cosine similarity is common for text. Attributes must be normalised first, otherwise a salary column dominates an age column.

Euclidean: d = sqrt( sum (xi - yi)^2 )
Manhattan: d = sum |xi - yi|
Minkowski: d = ( sum |xi - yi|^p )^(1/p)
Hamming:   number of positions that differ (binary/categorical)

Worked Example

Training points: (1,1) class A, (2,2) class A, (3,3) class B, (6,6) class B. Classify q = (2,1) with k = 3.

PointDistance to (2,1)ClassWeight 1/d
(1,1)1.000A1.000
(2,2)1.000A1.000
(3,3)2.236B0.447
(6,6)6.403B0.156

With k = 3 the neighbours are A, A and B, so unweighted voting predicts A. With weighted voting the A weight is 2.0 and the B weight is 0.447, again A. With k = 1 the nearest neighbour is A or B depending on the tie-break, which shows that small k is unstable.

Choosing k

  • Small k (1 to 3) follows local structure closely but is sensitive to noise and outliers.
  • Large k smooths the decision boundary but can mix classes and blur regions.
  • Choose k by cross-validation, commonly an odd number to avoid ties.
  • Weighted voting (weight = 1/distance) reduces the influence of distant neighbours.

Curse of Dimensionality

As the number of attributes grows, distances between points become nearly equal, so "nearest" loses meaning. k-NN therefore degrades in high dimensions unless attributes are reduced (PCA, attribute selection) or a domain-specific distance is used.

Strengths and Weaknesses

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple, no training phasePrediction scans the whole training set
Naturally handles multi-class problemsSensitive to irrelevant attributes and to scaling
Can learn complex, non-linear boundariesNeeds a good distance measure and a good k
Works with any number of classesSlow for very large datasets and high dimensions

Exam point: describe the algorithm, compute Euclidean distances for a tiny example, and explain the effect of k and of normalisation.

children.title: Neural Networks: Perceptron and Multilayer Networks
children.body:
The Artificial Neuron

A neuron takes several inputs xi, multiplies each by a weight wi, adds a bias b and passes the result through an activation function:

z = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wn xn + b
y = f(z)

The weights decide how much each input matters; the bias shifts the decision threshold. Learning means adjusting the weights so that the output matches the training labels.

Activation Functions

FunctionFormulaRangeUse
Step1 if z >= 0 else 0{0, 1}Classic perceptron
Sigmoid1 / (1 + e^(-z))(0, 1)Probability output, smooth
Tanh(e^z - e^(-z)) / (e^z + e^(-z))(-1, 1)Centred version of sigmoid
ReLUmax(0, z)[0, infinity)Deep networks, fast
Softmaxe^zi / sum e^zj(0, 1), sums to 1Multi-class output layer

The Perceptron

A single neuron with a step function can solve linearly separable problems. It updates weights after each mistake: wi = wi + learning_rate * (target - output) * xi. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees convergence only when the classes are linearly separable.

The classic failure is XOR: no single straight line separates (0,0), (1,1) from (0,1), (1,0). This limitation caused the first "AI winter" for neural networks.

Multilayer Networks

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) adds one or more hidden layers between input and output. Hidden layers transform the input into intermediate features, so the network can represent non-linear boundaries such as XOR. A network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function (universal approximation), although finding the right weights is the hard part.

input layer      hidden layer      output layer
  x1 o ---- w ---- o
              \  /   \
  x2 o --------- o ---- o  y
              /  \   /
  x3 o --------- o

(feed-forward: every neuron in one layer connects to the next)

Network Design Choices

  • Number of hidden layers and neurons: too few underfit, too many overfit and train slowly.
  • Activation: sigmoid or tanh for shallow networks, ReLU for deep ones.
  • Output: sigmoid for binary, softmax for multi-class, linear for regression.
  • Loss: cross-entropy for classification, mean squared error for regression.
  • Regularisation: weight decay, dropout, early stopping.

Strengths and Weaknesses

  • Strong on complex, high-dimensional and non-linear problems such as images and speech.
  • Tolerant of noisy input and can learn feature interactions automatically.
  • Training is slow and needs many records and careful tuning.
  • The learned weights are hard to interpret, and results vary with initialisation.

Exam point: draw a neuron and a small multilayer network, write the weighted-sum and sigmoid formulas, and explain why a single perceptron cannot solve XOR.

children.title: Backpropagation: Algorithm and Worked Example
children.body:
What Backpropagation Does

Backpropagation trains a multilayer network by gradient descent. It performs a forward pass to compute the output, computes the error, then propagates the error backwards through the layers to compute how much each weight contributed, and updates the weights in the direction that reduces the error.

Algorithm

  1. Initialise weights and biases to small random values.
  2. Forward pass: for each layer compute z = sum(w x) + b and the activation y = f(z) until the output is produced.
  3. Compute the error, for example E = 0.5 (target - output)^2 for one output, or cross-entropy for a classification layer.
  4. Output layer delta: delta_out = (target - output) * f'(z_out).
  5. Hidden layer delta: delta_h = (sum of delta_out * w) * f'(z_h), passed backwards layer by layer.
  6. Update each weight: w = w + learning_rate * delta * input_to_that_weight; update biases: b = b + learning_rate * delta.
  7. Repeat over the training set for many epochs until the error stops improving.

Worked Example: 2-1-1 Network

Inputs x1 = 0.5, x2 = 0.2. Hidden neuron h with weights wh1 = 0.4, wh2 = 0.6, bias bh = 0.1. Output neuron o with weight wo = 0.8, bias bo = 0.2. Sigmoid activation, learning rate 0.5, target t = 1.

forward, hidden:
  z_h = 0.4*0.5 + 0.6*0.2 + 0.1 = 0.42
  h   = sigmoid(0.42) = 0.6035

forward, output:
  z_o = 0.8*0.6035 + 0.2 = 0.6828
  o   = sigmoid(0.6828) = 0.6643

loss:
  E = 0.5 * (1 - 0.6643)^2 = 0.0564
backward:
  delta_o = (t - o) * o * (1 - o)
          = 0.3357 * 0.6643 * 0.3357 = 0.0749

  wo_new = 0.8 + 0.5 * 0.0749 * 0.6035 = 0.8226
  bo_new = 0.2 + 0.5 * 0.0749         = 0.2374

  delta_h = delta_o * wo * h * (1 - h)
          = 0.0749 * 0.8 * 0.6035 * 0.3965 = 0.0143

  wh1_new = 0.4 + 0.5 * 0.0143 * 0.5 = 0.4036
  wh2_new = 0.6 + 0.5 * 0.0143 * 0.2 = 0.6014
  bh_new  = 0.1 + 0.5 * 0.0143       = 0.1072

After one update the output moves slightly closer to 1. The process repeats for every training record and for many epochs; the error generally falls, although a bad learning rate can make it oscillate or diverge.

Role of the Learning Rate

  • Too small: training is very slow and may stall in a flat region.
  • Too large: the error oscillates or explodes because each update overshoots the minimum.
  • Common practice: start at 0.01 to 0.1 and decay it over time, or use an adaptive optimiser such as momentum or Adam.

Problems and Remedies

ProblemSymptomRemedy
OverfittingTraining error falls, validation error risesEarly stopping, dropout, weight decay, more data
Local minima / plateausTraining stallsMomentum, random restarts, ReLU
Vanishing gradientDeep layers learn very slowlyReLU, better initialisation, batch normalisation
Slow trainingMany epochs neededMini-batch gradient descent, adaptive learning rates

Exam point: write the forward pass, the delta formulas and the weight update for a tiny network. Show the sigmoid derivative o(1 - o); it is the step most often forgotten.

children.title: Confusion Matrix: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1
children.body:
The Confusion Matrix

For a two-class problem, every prediction falls into one of four cells. For the positive class "has the disease":

Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actual positiveTrue positive (TP)False negative (FN)
Actual negativeFalse positive (FP)True negative (TN)

A false positive is a false alarm; a false negative is a missed detection. In many applications the two kinds of error have very different costs.

The Metrics

Accuracy  = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN)
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)          how many flagged are actually positive
Recall     = TP / (TP + FN)          how many positives were found
F1         = 2 * P * R / (P + R)      harmonic mean of precision and recall
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)          how many negatives were correctly kept

Precision vs Recall trade-off:
  high precision = cautious classifier, few false alarms
  high recall    = eager classifier, finds almost all positives

Worked Example

A screening model on 200 records finds TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130.

Accuracy  = (40 + 130) / 200 = 0.850
Precision = 40 / (40 + 10)   = 0.800
Recall    = 40 / (40 + 20)   = 0.667
F1        = 2 * 0.8 * 0.667 / (0.8 + 0.667) = 0.727
Specificity = 130 / (130 + 10) = 0.929

The model finds two thirds of all sick people, and when it flags someone it is right 80 percent of the time. Accuracy alone (0.85) hides how many sick people were missed.

Why Accuracy Is Not Enough

With 99 percent healthy and 1 percent sick, a model that always predicts "healthy" is 99 percent accurate yet useless. Accuracy is only meaningful when classes are balanced and the two error types cost the same. This is why precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix itself are reported for imbalanced problems.

Choosing the Metric

GoalMetric to watchExample
Avoid false alarmsPrecisionSpam filter that must not delete real mail
Do not miss positivesRecallCancer screening, fraud detection
Balance bothF1General classifiers on imbalanced data
Overall correctness on balanced dataAccuracyDigit recognition

Multi-Class Version

For more than two classes, accuracy is still overall correctness. Precision and recall are computed per class (one-vs-rest) and averaged: macro-average gives each class equal weight, micro-average weights by the number of instances.

Exam point: define the four cells, write the four formulas and evaluate them on a given small confusion matrix. Explain the precision-recall trade-off.

children.title: ROC, AUC and Resampling Methods
children.body:
ROC Curves

Most classifiers can output a score or probability, not just a hard label. Changing the decision threshold moves the operating point along a trade-off between true positive rate (recall) and false positive rate:

TPR = TP / (TP + FN)   (sensitivity)
FPR = FP / (FP + TN)   (1 - specificity)

ROC plot: TPR on the y-axis, FPR on the x-axis, one point per threshold

TPR ^
   1 |                         x  perfect point (0, 1)
     |        x
     |   x
     | x
   0 +---------------------------> FPR
       0                       1
     the diagonal is random guessing; a good curve bows to the top-left

A useful model sits far above the diagonal. The perfect classifier passes through (0,1); a random classifier lies on the diagonal.

AUC

The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarises the whole curve in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random, and 0.9 is considered strong. AUC is threshold-independent and gives a fair comparison of different models over all operating points.

Evaluating on Held-Out Data

A model must be evaluated on records it never trained on. The standard methods:

  • Holdout: split once into training and test sets (for example 70/30). Simple, but the estimate depends on the single split.
  • Cross-validation: split into k folds, train on k-1 folds and test on the remaining one, rotating until every fold has been tested once. The result is the average over the k runs. Ten-fold is common.
  • Stratified cross-validation: each fold keeps the same class proportions as the whole dataset. Essential for imbalanced data.
  • Leave-one-out: k equals the number of records, so one record is tested per run. Accurate but expensive; used for small datasets.
  • Bootstrap: sample the data with replacement many times, train on each sample and test on the records left out.

Cross-Validation Worked Idea

With 10-fold cross-validation on 1,000 records, the data is cut into 10 blocks of 100. Run 1 trains on blocks 2 to 10 and tests on block 1; run 2 trains on all but block 2 and tests on block 2; and so on. Every record is tested exactly once, so the reported accuracy is the mean of the 10 run accuracies, with a standard deviation that shows how stable the model is.

Common Traps

  • Tuning hyperparameters on the test set leaks information. Use a separate validation set, or nested cross-validation.
  • Preprocessing (scaling, imputation) must be fitted inside each fold, not on the whole dataset.
  • Random k-fold breaks temporal order for time-series data; use forward-chaining splits instead.
  • Reporting the best fold instead of the average overstates performance.

Exam point: explain holdout, k-fold, stratified and leave-one-out; describe what the diagonal and the AUC mean on an ROC plot.

children.title: Clustering: Concepts, Requirements and Paradigms
children.body:
What Clustering Is

Clustering is an unsupervised task: it groups unlabelled objects so that objects in the same cluster are similar to each other and objects in different clusters are dissimilar. No class labels are used; the structure comes from the data itself. Clustering is also called unsupervised classification or segmentation.

Applications

  • Customer segmentation for marketing: groups with similar buying behaviour.
  • Document clustering for search and topic discovery.
  • Image segmentation and pattern recognition.
  • Anomaly detection: points that belong to no cluster are suspicious.
  • Biological taxonomy and gene expression analysis.

Requirements of a Good Clustering Method

  1. Scalability: works on large datasets, not just a few hundred rows.
  2. Mixed attribute types: handles numeric, categorical and text attributes.
  3. Arbitrary shapes: finds non-spherical clusters, not only round blobs.
  4. Domain constraints: can respect must-link and cannot-link rules.
  5. Noise tolerance: does not force every outlier into a cluster.
  6. Insensitivity to input order: the same data gives the same clusters.
  7. Interpretability: the clusters can be described and used.
  8. No need to guess k: ideally the number of clusters is discovered, not supplied.

Distance and Similarity

Every clustering algorithm depends on a proximity measure. Numeric data usually uses a distance (smaller means more similar); text and binary data often use a similarity (larger means more similar). The measure determines what "cluster" means, so it must be chosen for the domain.

Clustering Paradigms

ParadigmIdeaExamplesCluster shape
PartitioningSplit the data into k groups, optimising an objectivek-means, k-medoids (PAM, CLARA)Spherical, similar size
HierarchicalBuild a tree of nested clusters, bottom-up or top-downAGNES, DIANA, BIRCHAny, seen at a chosen level
Density-basedClusters are dense regions separated by sparse regionsDBSCAN, OPTICSArbitrary shapes, noise aware
Grid-basedQuantise space into cells and cluster the cellsSTING, CLIQUEFast for large data
Model-basedFit a probability model to each clusterGaussian mixture, EMElliptical, soft assignment

Hard vs Soft Clustering

Hard clustering assigns each object to exactly one cluster (k-means). Soft or fuzzy clustering gives each object a membership degree per cluster (fuzzy c-means, Gaussian mixtures), which is useful when boundaries are ambiguous.

Evaluating Clusters Without Labels

  • Compactness: points should be close to their own cluster centre (sum of squared errors).
  • Separation: cluster centres should be far apart.
  • Silhouette coefficient: compares the average distance to the own cluster with the average distance to the nearest other cluster; ranges from -1 to 1, higher is better.
  • Davies-Bouldin and Dunn indices: combine compactness and separation into one score.

Exam point: define clustering, list at least five requirements and name the main paradigms with one algorithm each. Mention that clustering is unsupervised and has no ground-truth labels.

children.title: Distance and Similarity Measures
children.body:
Minkowski Family

For numeric points x and y with n attributes, the Minkowski distance of order p is:

d(x, y) = ( sum |xi - yi|^p )^(1/p)

p = 1  Manhattan (city-block) distance
p = 2  Euclidean distance
p -> infinity  Chebyshev distance = max |xi - yi|

Euclidean is the default for geometric data. Manhattan is less sensitive to large single differences and is common in grid-like spaces. Chebyshev takes the largest single attribute difference.

Worked Example

Points A(1,1), B(2,4), C(4,3), D(5,6). Pairwise Euclidean distances:

Pair|dx| + |dy| (Manhattan)EuclideanChebyshev
A-B1 + 3 = 4sqrt(1 + 9) = 3.1623
A-C3 + 2 = 5sqrt(9 + 4) = 3.6063
A-D4 + 5 = 9sqrt(16 + 25) = 6.4035
B-C2 + 1 = 3sqrt(4 + 1) = 2.2362
B-D3 + 2 = 5sqrt(9 + 4) = 3.6063
C-D1 + 3 = 4sqrt(1 + 9) = 3.1623

This is the proximity matrix used by hierarchical clustering. Notice that the ordering of neighbours is similar for all three measures but not identical.

Cosine Similarity

For text and high-dimensional sparse vectors, angle matters more than length. Cosine similarity compares direction only:

cos(x, y) = (x . y) / ( |x| |y| )

x = (1, 0, 1, 1, 0), y = (1, 1, 0, 1, 0)
x . y = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2
|x| = sqrt(3) = 1.732,  |y| = sqrt(3) = 1.732
cos = 2 / 3 = 0.667
cosine distance = 1 - 0.667 = 0.333

Cosine ignores document length, which is why it dominates information retrieval and text clustering.

Jaccard Similarity

For binary or set data, Jaccard compares the size of the intersection with the size of the union:

J(A, B) = |A intersect B| / |A union B|

A = {bread, milk, eggs}, B = {milk, eggs, cola}
intersection = 2, union = 4, J = 0.5
Jaccard distance = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5

It treats shared presences as similarity and ignores shared absences, which makes it suitable for market baskets and sparse binary features.

Correlation and Other Measures

  • Pearson correlation: measures linear agreement of two numeric vectors; useful when the shape matters more than the magnitude.
  • Hamming distance: counts positions where two categorical or binary vectors differ.
  • Edit distance: number of insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one string into another.
  • Mahalanobis distance: accounts for the covariance between attributes, so correlated attributes are not double-counted.

Normalisation Before Distance

Distance is only meaningful when attributes are on comparable scales. If age ranges from 18 to 70 and income from 10,000 to 10,000,000, Euclidean distance is essentially the income difference. Normalise attributes (min-max or z-score) before clustering, and use the same transformation at prediction time.

Exam point: be able to compute Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine values for tiny examples, and explain why cosine is preferred for text.

children.title: Partitioning: k-Means and k-Medoids
children.body:
The Partitioning Idea

Partitioning methods divide n objects into k clusters, with k given in advance, by optimising an objective. Each cluster must contain at least one object, and every object belongs to exactly one cluster. The classic objective is the sum of squared errors (SSE), the total squared distance from each object to its cluster centre:

SSE = sum over clusters Cj, sum over objects x in Cj, || x - mj ||^2

where mj is the centre (mean) of cluster Cj. Lower SSE means tighter clusters.

k-Means Algorithm

  1. Choose k initial centres, for example k random objects or the result of a heuristic.
  2. Assign each object to the cluster whose centre is nearest.
  3. Recompute each centre as the mean of the objects assigned to it.
  4. Repeat assignment and update until the assignments stop changing or a maximum number of iterations is reached.
initial centres --> assign objects --> update means --> assign again
        ^                                              |
        +----------- stop when assignments are stable ---+

Worked Example

Four points: A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,3), D(5,4). Choose k = 2 with initial centres m1 = A = (1,1) and m2 = D = (5,4).

PointDistance to m1 (1,1)Distance to m2 (5,4)Assigned to
A (1,1)0.0005.000C1
B (2,1)1.0004.243C1
C (4,3)3.6061.414C2
D (5,4)5.0000.000C2

New centres: m1 = ((1+2)/2, (1+1)/2) = (1.5, 1); m2 = ((4+5)/2, (3+4)/2) = (4.5, 3.5). Reassign:

PointTo m1 (1.5,1)To m2 (4.5,3.5)Assigned to
A (1,1)0.5004.301C1
B (2,1)0.5003.640C1
C (4,3)3.2020.707C2
D (5,4)4.6100.707C2

The assignment did not change, so the algorithm stops. SSE = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.50.

Properties of k-Means

  • Fast and simple: O(n k t) for n objects, k clusters and t iterations.
  • Finds spherical clusters of similar size; fails on elongated or nested shapes.
  • Sensitive to the initial centres: a bad start can give a poor local optimum. k-means++ chooses spread-out initial centres to help.
  • Sensitive to outliers, because a mean is pulled by extreme values.
  • Requires k in advance and assumes numeric attributes (or a meaningful mean).
  • The result can change with the order of the data, so multiple restarts are common.

Choosing k

The elbow method plots SSE against k and looks for the point where extra clusters stop reducing error sharply. The silhouette coefficient measures how well each point fits its own cluster compared with the next nearest; average it over all points and choose the k with the highest score.

k-Medoids (PAM)

Instead of a mean, each cluster is represented by one of its actual objects, the medoid, chosen to minimise the total distance to the other members. Because a medoid is a real record, k-medoids works with arbitrary distance measures and is more robust to outliers.

k-means centre:  mean of members (may not be a real record)
k-medoids centre: an actual member (robust to outliers, works with any distance)

PAM (partitioning around medoids) tries swaps of a medoid with a non-medoid and keeps the swap that reduces the total cost, which is slower than k-means. CLARA samples the data to apply PAM to large datasets.

Exam point: write the k-means algorithm, perform one or two iterations on a small point set, compute SSE, and compare k-means with k-medoids.

children.title: Hierarchical and Density-Based Clustering
children.body:
Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical methods build a tree of nested clusters without being told k in advance. The result is a dendrogram: a tree whose leaves are the objects and whose internal nodes are merges (agglomerative) or splits (divisive). Cutting the dendrogram at a chosen height produces a flat clustering.

Agglomerative (AGNES)

  1. Start with each object in its own cluster.
  2. Compute the distance between every pair of clusters.
  3. Merge the two closest clusters.
  4. Update distances and repeat until one cluster remains.

Divisive (DIANA)

Start with one cluster containing all objects and repeatedly split the cluster whose split improves cohesion the most, until every object is alone. Divisive methods are more expensive because they consider many possible splits.

Linkage Methods

LinkageDistance between clustersBehaviour
Single (nearest neighbour)Minimum distance between any two membersCan follow long chains; sensitive to noise
Complete (farthest neighbour)Maximum distance between any two membersCompact clusters; sensitive to outliers
AverageAverage distance over all pairsBalanced compromise
CentroidDistance between cluster meansCan invert the merge order
WardIncrease in within-cluster varianceCompact, similar-size clusters

Worked Merge Order

Using the points and Euclidean distances from the distance-measure note: A(1,1), B(2,4), C(4,3), D(5,6). Closest pair is B-C at 2.236, so merge {B,C}. Distances from {B,C} to A: single linkage min(3.162, 3.606) = 3.162; to D: min(3.606, 3.162) = 3.162. Next closest pair is {A} and {B,C} or {D} and {B,C}, both 3.162; a tie is broken arbitrarily. If {A} joins, the final merge with D happens at 6.403.

dendrogram (heights are merge distances)

6.4 |                       +-----+
3.2 |             +---------+     |
2.2 |       +-----+               |
    |   A   B     C               D
    +-------------------------------->

Density-Based Clustering: DBSCAN

Density-based methods define clusters as regions of high density separated by regions of low density. They can find arbitrary shapes and explicitly label noise, which partitioning and hierarchical methods cannot.

Two parameters: eps (neighbourhood radius) and minPts (minimum neighbours to be dense). Every point is one of:

  • Core point: has at least minPts points within eps (including itself).
  • Border point: has fewer than minPts neighbours but lies within eps of a core point.
  • Noise point: neither core nor border.
algorithm:
  for each unvisited point p
    if p is a core point
      create a cluster, add p and all density-reachable points
    else mark p as noise (it may later become a border point)

DBSCAN Worked Example

Points A(1,1), B(1.4,1), C(1.8,1), D(4,4), E(4.4,4), F(4.8,4), G(9,9) with eps = 1 and minPts = 3. A, B and C are mutually within 1, so each has three neighbours and they form one cluster. D, E and F likewise form a second cluster. G has no neighbour within 1, so it is noise. Note that a single point can be a border point of two clusters only if it is within eps of core points from both; DBSCAN assigns it to the first cluster that reaches it.

Choosing eps and minPts

A common heuristic plots the distance to the k-th nearest neighbour (k = minPts) for every point, sorts the values and looks for a knee; eps is set near the knee. minPts is often at least the number of dimensions plus one, and larger for noisy data.

Comparison

MethodNeeds kCluster shapeNoise handlingCost
k-meansYesSphericalNone (outliers distort means)Low
HierarchicalNo (cut later)Any, depends on linkagePoor without pruningMedium to high
DBSCANNo (needs eps, minPts)ArbitraryExplicit noise labelMedium, needs spatial index

Exam point: draw a dendrogram and explain the three linkage types; define core, border and noise points and walk through DBSCAN on a small set.

children.title: Choosing and Evaluating a Classifier
children.body:
Bias and Variance

Bias is error from a model that is too simple to capture the pattern (underfitting). Variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training sample (overfitting). The test error is roughly bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. As model complexity grows, bias falls and variance rises, so the best model sits at the point where total error is lowest.

error
  | \                 /
  |  \   variance   /
  |   \            /
  |    \    total /
  |     \      /
  |      \  /
  |       V  <- sweet spot
  +----------------------> model complexity
     bias high            variance high

Algorithm Cheat Sheet

SituationReasonable first choiceWhy
Need an explainable modelDecision tree or rule learnerRules can be read and audited
Many attributes, text dataNaive Bayes or linear SVMFast and strong on sparse data
Small dataset, simple boundaryLogistic regression or naive BayesLittle data to overfit
Non-linear boundary, enough dataRandom forest or neural networkLearns interactions
Mixed numeric and categoricalTree ensembleHandles both without scaling
Find groups, no labelsk-means, then hierarchical or DBSCANFast start, then check shape

Handling Imbalanced Classes

  • Use stratified splits so the test set keeps the minority class.
  • Report precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix, not accuracy alone.
  • Resample the training set: oversample the minority, undersample the majority, or use SMOTE to synthesise minority points.
  • Weight the minority class more heavily in the loss function.
  • Move the decision threshold instead of accepting the default 0.5.

Ensembles in One Paragraph

Bagging trains many models on bootstrap samples and averages them; it mainly reduces variance (random forests). Boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on the errors of the previous one; it mainly reduces bias (AdaBoost, gradient boosting). Stacking combines the outputs of several models with a meta-learner. Ensembles usually beat a single model, at the cost of interpretability and training time.

Practical Checklist

  1. Define the target and the cost of each error before choosing a metric.
  2. Clean and split the data (stratified, or chronological for time series).
  3. Fit preprocessing on the training fold only.
  4. Establish a simple baseline (majority class, logistic regression) before trying complex models.
  5. Compare models with cross-validation and report mean and spread.
  6. Tune a few hyperparameters with a validation set, not the test set.
  7. Inspect errors, not just scores: look at misclassified examples and class-wise metrics.
  8. Check that the model can be applied to new records with the same transformations.

Clustering in Practice

  • Normalise attributes before distance-based clustering.
  • Scale or remove attributes that are irrelevant; they add noise to every distance.
  • Run k-means several times with different seeds and keep the solution with the lowest SSE.
  • Choose k with the elbow or silhouette, and check that the clusters make domain sense.
  • Use DBSCAN when clusters may have arbitrary shapes or when noise must be labelled.
  • Describe each cluster by its centre and by the attributes that differ most from the global mean.

Exam point: explain bias-variance with the curve, and give three concrete techniques for imbalanced classification.

children.title: Important Definitions and Quick Revision
children.body:
Important Definitions

  • Classification: supervised learning of a model that assigns a categorical label to new records.
  • Prediction: supervised estimation of a continuous target value.
  • Training set: labelled records used to build the model.
  • Test set: held-out labelled records used to estimate accuracy.
  • Overfitting: fitting noise in the training data so that test performance falls.
  • Pruning: removing tree branches that do not improve generalisation.
  • Entropy: a measure of class impurity, H(S) = -sum pi log2 pi.
  • Information gain: the reduction in entropy achieved by splitting on an attribute.
  • Gain ratio: information gain divided by split information; used by C4.5.
  • Gini index: 1 - sum pi^2; used by CART to measure impurity.
  • Naive Bayes: a Bayesian classifier that assumes conditional independence of attributes given the class.
  • Laplace smoothing: adding a small count to avoid zero probabilities.
  • k-NN: a lazy classifier that predicts from the majority class of the k nearest training records.
  • Perceptron: a single neuron with a step activation and a linear decision boundary.
  • Backpropagation: gradient-descent training of a multilayer network by propagating output error backwards.
  • Confusion matrix: a table of TP, FP, FN and TN counts.
  • Precision: TP / (TP + FP).
  • Recall: TP / (TP + FN).
  • F1: the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
  • ROC curve: TPR versus FPR over all thresholds.
  • AUC: area under the ROC curve; 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is random.
  • Cross-validation: rotating training and test folds to estimate performance.
  • Clustering: unsupervised grouping of similar objects.
  • k-means: partitioning clustering that minimises the sum of squared distances to cluster means.
  • k-medoids: partitioning clustering that uses actual objects as cluster centres.
  • Dendrogram: a tree diagram of hierarchical merges or splits.
  • DBSCAN: density-based clustering that labels core, border and noise points.
  • Silhouette coefficient: a compactness-and-separation score between -1 and 1.

Important Formulas

entropy:       H(S) = -sum pi log2 pi
information gain: Gain(A) = H(S) - sum (|Sv|/|S|) H(Sv)
gain ratio:    Gain(A) / SplitInfo(A)
Gini:          Gini(S) = 1 - sum pi^2
sigmoid:       f(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z),  f'(z) = f(z)(1 - f(z))
weight update: w = w + learning_rate * delta * input
accuracy:      (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN)
precision:     TP / (TP + FP)
recall:        TP / (TP + FN)
F1:            2PR / (P + R)
SSE:           sum over clusters, sum over points || x - m ||^2
Minkowski:     ( sum |xi - yi|^p )^(1/p)
cosine:        (x . y) / (|x| |y|)
Jaccard:       |A intersect B| / |A union B|

Important Comparisons

  1. Classification vs prediction vs clustering.
  2. ID3 vs C4.5 vs CART.
  3. Information gain vs Gini index.
  4. Pre-pruning vs post-pruning.
  5. Naive Bayes vs k-NN.
  6. Perceptron vs multilayer perceptron.
  7. Accuracy vs precision vs recall vs F1.
  8. Holdout vs k-fold vs leave-one-out cross-validation.
  9. k-means vs k-medoids.
  10. Hierarchical vs partitioning vs density-based clustering.
  11. Single vs complete vs average linkage.
  12. Hard vs soft clustering.
  13. Overfitting vs underfitting.

Important Diagrams to Practise

  1. The two-step classification process.
  2. A decision tree for the play dataset.
  3. The entropy and information-gain calculation table.
  4. A confusion matrix with its four cells.
  5. An ROC curve with the diagonal and the AUC area.
  6. A multilayer perceptron with one hidden layer.
  7. The backpropagation forward and backward pass.
  8. k-means before and after the centroid update.
  9. A dendrogram with a cut line.
  10. Core, border and noise points for DBSCAN.

Important Long-Answer Questions

  1. Explain the general approach to classification with a diagram.
  2. Explain decision tree induction and attribute selection by information gain.
  3. Compute information gain and Gini index for a given dataset and construct the tree.
  4. Compare ID3, C4.5 and CART.
  5. Explain overfitting and pruning in decision trees.
  6. Explain naive Bayes classification with a worked example and Laplace smoothing.
  7. Explain k-NN and the effect of k, distance measure and normalisation.
  8. Explain the perceptron and multilayer neural networks; why can a perceptron not solve XOR?
  9. Explain backpropagation with the forward pass, delta computation and weight update.
  10. Explain accuracy, precision, recall and F1 with a confusion matrix.
  11. Explain ROC, AUC and cross-validation.
  12. Explain k-means with a worked example; compare it with k-medoids.
  13. Explain hierarchical clustering with linkage methods and a dendrogram.
  14. Explain DBSCAN with core, border and noise points.

Important Short-Answer Questions

  1. Define classification.
  2. What is a training set?
  3. What is overfitting?
  4. Define entropy.
  5. State the information gain formula.
  6. What is the Gini index?
  7. What is gain ratio and why is it needed?
  8. State Bayes theorem.
  9. What is the naive independence assumption?
  10. What is Laplace smoothing?

  17. Define clustering.
  18. What is a dendrogram?

  21. What is the curse of dimensionality?

Study Strategy

  • Practise the entropy and Gini calculations until the arithmetic is quick and accurate.
  • Memorise the four confusion-matrix metrics and be able to compute them from a 2 x 2 table.
  • Draw the two-step classification diagram and the perceptron diagram from memory.
  • Work through the naive Bayes example and the backpropagation example once by hand.
  • For clustering, memorise the k-means loop, the three linkage types, and the DBSCAN point types.
  • Remember which algorithm uses which measure: ID3 gain, C4.5 gain ratio, CART Gini.
  • Link evaluation to real costs: a false negative in medical screening matters more than a false positive.
  • Practise one numerical question per topic; Module 3 exams are calculation-heavy.

modules.title: Module 4: Association Rule Analysis and Advanced Data Mining
modules.subtitle: PECST525 | Data Mining

children.title: Market Basket Analysis and Rule Measures
children.body:
What Association Rule Mining Is

Association rule mining finds items that occur together in transactions: "customers who buy bread and milk also buy diapers". It is the classic market basket analysis technique and is also used for web clickstreams, medical records, recommender systems and intrusion detection.

The input is a set of transactions, each a subset of items. A rule has the form X -> Y, where X and Y are disjoint itemsets. X is the antecedent (the "if" part) and Y is the consequent (the "then" part).

The Three Core Measures

Support, confidence and lift are computed from counts over the transaction database:

support(X -> Y)    = count(X union Y) / N        how often the rule applies
confidence(X -> Y) = count(X union Y) / count(X)  how reliable the rule is
lift(X -> Y)       = confidence / support(Y)
                   = support(X union Y) / (support(X) support(Y))
  • Support measures frequency. A rule with low support may be a coincidence.
  • Confidence measures reliability: the fraction of transactions with X that also have Y.
  • Lift measures whether Y is more likely given X than it is in general. Lift > 1 means positive association, lift = 1 means independence, lift < 1 means the items repel each other.

Worked Example

Five transactions: T1 = {bread, milk}, T2 = {bread, diaper, beer, eggs}, T3 = {milk, diaper, beer, cola}, T4 = {bread, milk, diaper, beer}, T5 = {bread, milk, diaper, cola}.

Rule: bread -> milk.

count(bread) = 4, count(milk) = 4, count(bread, milk) = 3, N = 5

support    = 3/5 = 0.60  (60 percent of all transactions)
confidence = 3/4 = 0.75  (75 percent of bread buyers also buy milk)
lift       = 0.75 / (4/5) = 0.9375  (< 1: slightly negative association)

The lift below 1 is instructive: milk is bought in 80 percent of transactions overall, so buying bread actually makes milk slightly less likely than usual. Confidence alone would have made the rule look strong.

Frequent Itemsets

A rule can only be strong if its itemset occurs often. Mining therefore works in two steps: find all frequent itemsets whose support is at least a minimum threshold (minsup), then generate rules from them whose confidence is at least a minimum threshold (minconf).

The number of possible itemsets is 2^m for m items, so brute force is impossible even for a few hundred items. The Apriori property makes the search tractable: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent, and every superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent.

Applications

  • Retail: product placement, cross-selling, promotions.
  • Web: pages visited together, adaptive site design.
  • Medicine: symptoms and diagnoses that co-occur.
  • Recommenders: "customers who bought this also bought".
  • Intrusion detection: unusual combinations of system calls.

Exam point: define support, confidence and lift, compute all three for a small transaction set, and explain why lift is needed in addition to confidence.

children.title: Interestingness Measures
children.body:
Why Support and Confidence Are Not Enough

Support and confidence are the original measures, but confidence can be high for a rule that is useless. If 90 percent of transactions contain milk, then any rule X -> milk has confidence of at least 0.9 without X telling us anything. The rule is not interesting; it simply reflects a popular item.

An interestingness measure quantifies how much the antecedent changes the likelihood of the consequent. Lift is the simplest; several others are used when the data is sparse or imbalanced.

Common Measures

MeasureFormulaInterpretation
Supportcount(X u Y) / NFrequency of the rule
Confidencecount(X u Y) / count(X)Reliability of the rule
Liftconfidence / support(Y)> 1 positive, 1 independent, < 1 negative
Leveragesupport(X u Y) - support(X) support(Y)Absolute excess co-occurrence
Conviction(1 - support(Y)) / (1 - confidence)How often X occurs without Y
Cosinesupport(X u Y) / sqrt(support(X) support(Y))Symmetric, bounded 0 to 1
All-confidencesupport(X u Y) / max(support(X), support(Y))Bounded by the weaker support
Kulczynski0.5 (support(X u Y)/support(X) + support(X u Y)/support(Y))Average conditional probability

Worked Comparison

Using the same database, rule bread -> milk has support 0.60, confidence 0.75, support(milk) = 0.80:

lift      = 0.75 / 0.80 = 0.9375
leverage  = 0.60 - (0.80)(0.80) = 0.60 - 0.64 = -0.04
conviction = (1 - 0.80) / (1 - 0.75) = 0.20 / 0.25 = 0.80
cosine    = 0.60 / sqrt(0.80 * 0.80) = 0.75

All four say the same thing: the association is not positive. Conviction below 1 means the rule is violated more often than independence would predict.

The Null-Invariance Problem

In sparse data, most items are absent from most transactions. Measures that count shared absences can look large even when the items never appear together. Lift and cosine are null-invariant (they ignore transactions containing neither item); leverage and chi-square are not. For market baskets and text, null-invariant measures such as Kulczynski and cosine are usually more trustworthy.

A practical approach is to report several measures rather than one. A rule is described as interesting when support is above a business minimum, confidence is high, and lift (or another null-invariant measure) is clearly above 1.

Objective vs Subjective Interestingness

  • Objective: computed from counts alone (support, confidence, lift, chi-square).
  • Subjective: depends on the user's prior knowledge: a rule is interesting if it is unexpected. A rule stating that "people who buy a car also buy insurance" is strong but unsurprising, so a domain expert may call it uninteresting.

Exam point: explain the weakness of confidence with an example, define lift, and list three alternative measures with their formulas.

children.title: Apriori: Candidate Generation and Pruning
children.body:
The Apriori Property

Apriori is built on one observation: if an itemset is frequent, every subset of it is frequent; if an itemset is infrequent, every superset of it is infrequent. The second form is the useful one: once {beer, cola} is known to be infrequent, no larger itemset containing both can be frequent, so the whole branch is pruned.

Level-Wise Search

  1. Scan the database to count single items; keep those with support at least minsup. This is L1.
  2. Generate candidate pairs from L1, count them with another scan, and keep frequent pairs as L2.
  3. Generate candidate triples by joining frequent pairs that share their first item, prune candidates with an infrequent subset, count the rest, and keep L3.
  4. Repeat until no candidate survives.
C1 -> L1 -> C2 -> L2 -> C3 -> L3 -> ...
         (count)   (count)   (count)
  pruning uses the Apriori property at every level

Worked Example

Five transactions, minsup = 2 transactions (40 percent). Items are kept in the fixed order bread, milk, diaper, beer, cola.

T1 = bread, milk
T2 = bread, diaper, beer, eggs
T3 = milk, diaper, beer, cola
T4 = bread, milk, diaper, beer
T5 = bread, milk, diaper, cola

Level 1

L1 = {bread, milk, diaper, beer, cola}. Eggs is dropped and never appears again.

Level 2

CandidateCountFrequent?
bread, milk3yes
bread, diaper3yes
bread, beer2yes
bread, cola1no
milk, diaper3yes
milk, beer2yes

L2 has eight itemsets. Note that {bread, cola} and {beer, cola} are pruned now; no larger itemset containing them is ever generated.

Level 3

Join pairs that share their first item: {bread, milk} with {bread, diaper} gives {bread, milk, diaper}; and so on. Then prune candidates that contain an infrequent pair: {bread, milk, cola} is removed because {bread, cola} is not in L2.

CandidateSubset checkCountResult

L3 = {bread, milk, diaper}, {bread, diaper, beer}, {milk, diaper, beer}, {milk, diaper, cola}.

Level 4

Joining L3 itemsets that share their first two items gives {bread, milk, diaper, beer} and {milk, diaper, beer, cola}. Both contain an infrequent triple ({bread, milk, beer} and {milk, beer, cola} respectively), so both are pruned before counting. No frequent 4-itemset exists and the algorithm stops.

Cost

Apriori scans the database once per level, so it needs k full scans to find frequent itemsets up to size k. Candidate generation can be large, and counting every candidate with a database scan is expensive for dense data with long itemsets. These costs motivate the improvements and FP-growth.

Exam point: show C1, L1, C2, L2, C3 and L3 for a small database. State the Apriori property explicitly and show at least one candidate pruned by subset check and one pruned by count.

children.title: Rule Generation and Apriori Improvements
children.body:
Generating Rules from a Frequent Itemset

For every frequent itemset Z and every non-empty proper subset X of Z, form the rule X -> (Z - X). Its confidence is support(Z) / support(X). Keep the rule if confidence is at least minconf.

Rules from {bread, milk, diaper} with support 0.4 and minconf 0.5:

RuleConfidenceKept?
bread -> milk, diaper2/4 = 0.50yes
milk -> bread, diaper2/4 = 0.50yes
diaper -> bread, milk2/4 = 0.50yes
bread, milk -> diaper2/3 = 0.67yes
bread, diaper -> milk2/3 = 0.67yes
milk, diaper -> bread2/3 = 0.67yes

The confidence of a rule increases as the consequent shrinks: dropping an item from the consequent cannot lower confidence, because the antecedent stays the same or grows. This monotonicity lets rule generation prune too: if X -> Y does not meet minconf, no rule with a smaller consequent derived from the same itemset can meet it.

Apriori Improvement 1: Partitioning

Divide the database into blocks that fit in memory and find local frequent itemsets in each block. Any globally frequent itemset must be locally frequent in at least one block, so the union of local frequent itemsets is a superset of the global ones. A final scan counts the candidates on the full database. Two scans instead of k, at the cost of many candidates.

Apriori Improvement 2: Sampling

Mine a random sample and verify the rules on the full data. Fast and usually accurate, but a rule that is frequent only in the unsampled part can be missed. Often used to find a lower support threshold for the full run.

Apriori Improvement 3: DHP (Hashing)

During the count of L1, hash pairs into buckets and count bucket sizes. Buckets below minsup cannot contain a frequent pair, so many C2 candidates are eliminated without counting them. DHP reduces the candidate set substantially for the second level.

Apriori Improvement 4: Vertical Formats

Store each item with the list of transactions that contain it (a tidset) instead of scanning rows. Support of an itemset is the size of the intersection of tidsets, and intersections are fast. Eclat uses this idea with depth-first search.

Comparison

MethodIdeaStrengthWeakness
AprioriLevel-wise candidate generationSimple, correctMany scans, many candidates
PartitionLocal mining then global verificationTwo scansLarge candidate union
SamplingMine a sampleFastMay miss rare rules
DHPHash-based candidate pruningFewer C2 candidatesExtra memory
EclatVertical tidsetsFast support countingLarge intersections for dense data

Exam point: generate rules from a frequent itemset and compute confidence; then name three improvements to Apriori and one limitation of each.

children.title: FP-Tree Construction
children.body:
Why FP-Growth

Apriori repeatedly scans the database and generates a huge number of candidates. FP-growth (frequent pattern growth) scans the database twice, compresses it into a prefix tree called an FP-tree, and then mines the tree without generating candidates. It is usually much faster on dense data.

Step 1: Count and Order Items

Scan the database once to count item frequencies. Discard items below minsup, then sort the remaining items in decreasing frequency. Every transaction is rewritten in that order, with infrequent items removed.

Same five transactions, minsup = 2:

TransactionOriginalSorted (frequent items only)
T1bread, milkbread, milk
T2bread, diaper, beer, eggsbread, diaper, beer
T3milk, diaper, beer, colamilk, diaper, beer, cola
T4bread, milk, diaper, beerbread, milk, diaper, beer
T5bread, milk, diaper, colabread, milk, diaper, cola

Step 2: Build the Tree

Insert each sorted transaction as a path from the root, sharing prefixes with existing paths and incrementing counts along the way. A header table links every item to all its nodes in the tree.

root

      +-- milk:3
      |    +-- diaper:2
      |         +-- beer:1
      |         +-- cola:1
      +-- diaper:1

      +-- diaper:1
