                +-- cola:1
ItemFrequencyLinked nodes (path: count)
bread4root/bread:4
milk4bread/milk:3, root/milk:1
diaper4bread/milk/diaper:2, bread/diaper:1, milk/diaper:1
beer3bread/milk/diaper/beer:1, bread/diaper/beer:1, milk/diaper/beer:1
cola2bread/milk/diaper/cola:1, milk/diaper/beer/cola:1

Properties of the FP-Tree

  • The tree is compact: shared prefixes are stored once, so the size is bounded by the number of frequent items, not by the number of transactions.
  • It is complete: every transaction is represented, with counts preserving support.
  • It never contains an infrequent item, because those were removed before insertion.
  • It preserves only the order of items; the original transaction boundaries are recoverable by following root-to-node paths.
  • Building needs exactly two database scans: one to count, one to insert.

Exam point: given a small transaction database and minsup, draw the FP-tree with counts and the header table. Show the sorted transactions first; the ordering step is where most mistakes happen.

children.title: Mining Frequent Itemsets from an FP-Tree
children.body:
Conditional Pattern Bases

FP-growth processes items from the least frequent upwards. For an item, collect every path from the root to a node of that item. Each path becomes a conditional pattern base: the prefix before the item, with the count of that item node. Then build a small conditional FP-tree from those prefixes, keeping only items whose cumulative count reaches minsup.

For cola (frequency 2), the two paths are:

bread -> milk -> diaper -> cola    gives prefix {bread, milk, diaper}: 1
milk -> diaper -> beer -> cola     gives prefix {milk, diaper, beer}: 1

cumulative counts in the base: bread 1, milk 2, diaper 2, beer 1
minsup 2 keeps milk and diaper, so the conditional tree is:
  milk:2 -> diaper:2

Mining this conditional tree gives {milk, cola}:2, {diaper, cola}:2 and the combined {milk, diaper, cola}:2, exactly the frequent itemsets containing cola.

A Second Example: diaper

The prefix paths containing diaper are {bread, milk}:2, {milk}:1 and {bread}:1. Counts are bread 3 and milk 3, but the shared prefix matters: the conditional tree keeps bread:3 with a milk:2 child plus a separate milk:1 node. The resulting itemsets are {bread, diaper}:3, {milk, diaper}:3 and {bread, milk, diaper}:2. The last one has support 2, not 3, because only two transactions contain all three items; this shows why the conditional tree preserves structure instead of just totals.

Recursive Mining

  1. Take an item from the header table, starting with the least frequent.
  2. Build its conditional pattern base and conditional FP-tree.
  3. If the conditional tree contains a single path, enumerate all combinations of that path with the item and stop.
  4. Otherwise recurse on each item in the conditional tree.
  5. Continue until every item has been processed, collecting all frequent itemsets.

Why There Are No Candidate Sets

Apriori generates candidates and tests them. FP-growth grows itemsets directly from the compressed tree, so it never proposes an itemset that is not supported by some path. The Apriori property is still at work: a path that does not meet minsup is never followed.

FP-Growth vs Apriori

AspectAprioriFP-growth
Database scansOne per level, k scansTwo scans total
CandidatesGenerates and tests manyNone, grows from the tree
Main data structureLevel-wise itemset listsFP-tree in memory
Speed on dense dataSlowMuch faster
MemoryLowerHigher, the tree must fit in memory
ImplementationSimpleMore complex

Limitations

  • The FP-tree must fit in main memory; very large or very dense databases may not.
  • The tree can be large when many items are frequent and transactions share few prefixes.
  • Support is still the only pruning criterion, so the quality of the resulting rules depends on the interestingness measures used afterwards.

Exam point: build a conditional pattern base and conditional FP-tree for one item, then list the frequent itemsets it produces. Compare FP-growth with Apriori in a table.

children.title: Closed, Maximal and Constrained Patterns
children.body:
Too Many Frequent Itemsets

On dense data, the number of frequent itemsets explodes: 100 frequent items can produce an enormous number of combinations. Many of them carry the same information, because if an itemset is frequent then all its subsets are frequent too. Two compressed representations keep only the informative itemsets.

Closed Itemsets

An itemset is closed if none of its immediate supersets has the same support. Equivalently, adding any item reduces the support. Closed itemsets preserve all support information: the support of any itemset equals the support of the smallest closed itemset containing it.

Maximal Itemsets

An itemset is maximal frequent if it is frequent and none of its supersets is frequent. Maximal itemsets are a smaller set than closed itemsets and give a compact picture of the frequent region, but they lose exact support values: an itemset that is not maximal has unknown support unless it is also closed.

RepresentationDefinitionKeeps all supports?Size
All frequent itemsetsEvery itemset at or above minsupYesLargest
Closed itemsetsFrequent, and no superset has the same supportYesSmaller
Maximal itemsetsFrequent, and no superset is frequentNoSmallest

Example: if {bread, milk, diaper} has support 2 and {bread, milk} also has support 2, then {bread, milk} is not closed. If no frequent itemset contains {bread, milk, diaper}, it is both closed and maximal.

Constraint-Based Pattern Mining

Users often want patterns that satisfy conditions beyond support: only rules about a category, only itemsets containing a target item, only patterns above a price threshold. Constraint-based mining pushes these conditions into the search so that useless patterns are never generated.

  • Anti-monotone constraints: if an itemset satisfies the constraint, every subset does (for example, total price at most 100). These prune like support.
  • Monotone constraints: if an itemset satisfies the constraint, every superset does (for example, contains "beer").
  • Succinct constraints: the set of satisfying itemsets can be enumerated directly (for example, items from a given list).
  • Convertible constraints: become anti-monotone after reordering items (for example, average price above a threshold).

A constraint such as "contains exactly one brand" is neither monotone nor anti-monotone and is harder to push; the usual approach is to mine with support and filter afterwards.

Why Compression Matters

Closed and maximal mining produce far fewer patterns for the same data, which makes the output usable and the algorithm faster. The trade-off is that the analyst must understand which representation keeps the information needed for the question.

Exam point: define closed and maximal itemsets with a small example, state which one preserves support, and give one monotone and one anti-monotone constraint.

children.title: Sequential Patterns and Association-Based Classification
children.body:
From Itemsets to Sequences

Market-basket rules ignore order. A sequential pattern captures order: customers who buy a phone, then a case, then a charger. The data is a set of sequences of transactions, each sequence ordered in time. A sequence is frequent if it appears in at least minsup percent of the sequences.

customer 1: <{phone}> <{case, screen guard}> <{charger}>
customer 2: <{phone}> <{charger}>
customer 3: <{laptop}> <{mouse}>

pattern: <{phone}> <{charger}>  appears in 2 of 3 sequences

Generalised Sequential Pattern (GSP)

GSP is the sequential version of Apriori. It generates candidate sequences, scans the data to count them and prunes using the property that every subsequence of a frequent sequence is frequent. PrefixSpan avoids candidate generation by projecting the database on prefixes, much as FP-growth does for itemsets.

Association-Based Classification

Association rules can be used for classification (association classification or CAR mining). Rules are mined with the class label as the consequent, for example "age young and student yes -> buys computer yes". The classifier then ranks rules by support and confidence and applies the best matching rule to a new record.

  • Rules are readable and can mix attributes in ways a tree cannot.
  • Mining all class rules can be expensive, and many rules may apply to the same record.
  • A common solution keeps only the top k rules per class and resolves conflicts by confidence, then by support.

Multi-Level Association Rules

With a concept hierarchy, rules can be mined at different levels: "bread -> milk" at the item level, "bakery -> dairy" at the category level. Multi-level mining finds strong rules that are rare at the fine level but common at the coarse level, and reduces the sparsity problem of long-tail items.

Other Pattern Families

Pattern typeAddsExample
Sequential patternOrder of eventsPhone then charger
Subgraph patternRelations between objectsFrequent social network structures
Periodic patternRegular repetitionWeekly purchase cycle
Negative patternItems that rarely co-occurCustomers who buy A avoid B
Uncertain patternProbabilistic transactionsSensor readings with confidence

Exam point: define a sequential pattern and compare GSP with PrefixSpan; explain how association rules can be turned into a classifier.

children.title: Web Mining: Taxonomy and Challenges
children.body:
What Web Mining Is

Web mining applies data mining techniques to web data in order to discover patterns about users, content and the link structure of the web. It combines ideas from databases, information retrieval, machine learning and natural language processing.

The Three Categories

CategoryData usedTypical tasks
Web content miningText, images, audio, video, structured markup on pagesClassification, clustering, extraction, summarisation
Web structure miningHyperlinks and the link graphPageRank, HITS, community discovery, link prediction
Web usage miningServer logs, clickstreams, queriesSession analysis, association rules, personalisation, recommendation

Web Content Mining

Content mining treats a page as a document. Tasks include classifying pages by topic, clustering similar pages, extracting structured records (prices, addresses) from HTML, and summarising or filtering text. The main difficulty is that HTML mixes content with layout and navigation, so boilerplate must be removed first.

Web Structure Mining

Structure mining uses links as votes or as evidence of relatedness. A page linked by many important pages is itself important (PageRank); a page that links to many good pages is a good hub (HITS). Link analysis is also used to find communities and to detect link spam.

Web Usage Mining

Usage mining analyses what users actually did: page views, clicks, search queries and timestamps. The raw log is noisy and must be cleaned and divided into user sessions before patterns can be found. Results feed recommender systems, adaptive sites, caching policy and marketing.

Challenges of Web Data

  • Scale: billions of pages and enormous logs; algorithms must be distributed.
  • Heterogeneity: pages mix text, images, scripts and structured data with no common schema.
  • Semi-structured and unstructured content: HTML is designed for rendering, not for extraction.
  • Dynamic content: pages change, disappear and are generated on request.
  • Link spam and manipulation: links and reviews can be bought, so naive trust in structure fails.
  • Privacy: usage logs contain personal behaviour and must be anonymised and handled lawfully.
  • Noise in logs: crawlers, caches and shared IP addresses distort user identification.

The Web Mining Pipeline

web sources (pages, links, logs)
   -> collection (crawling, log gathering)
   -> preprocessing (cleaning, parsing, session identification)
   -> pattern discovery (classification, clustering, rules, link analysis)
   -> pattern analysis (validation, visualisation, interpretation)
   -> application (recommendation, personalisation, ranking)

Exam point: draw the three-branch taxonomy with one task per branch, then list at least four challenges of web data.

children.title: Web Content and Structure Mining
children.body:
Content Mining Tasks

  • Classification: assign a topic or spam label to a page using naive Bayes, SVM or a neural network on the page text.
  • Clustering: group pages with similar content for topic discovery or duplicate detection.
  • Information extraction: pull structured facts (product, price, date) from HTML using rules, wrappers or learned extractors.
  • Summarisation: produce a short summary of a page or a set of pages on the same topic.

Structure Mining: PageRank

PageRank treats a link from page T to page A as a vote for A. Votes from important pages count more, and a page that spreads its votes over many outlinks gives less to each. With damping factor d (usually 0.85):

PR(A) = (1 - d) + d * sum over pages T linking to A of ( PR(T) / C(T) )

C(T) = number of outlinks from T
(1 - d) models a random jump to any page

PageRank Worked Example

Three pages: A links to B and C; B links to C; C links to A. Start with PR = 1 for every page.

IterationPR(A)PR(B)PR(C)Sum
start1.0001.0001.0003.000
10.150 + 0.85 x 1.000 = 1.0000.150 + 0.85 x 0.500 = 0.5750.150 + 0.85 x (0.500 + 1.000) = 1.4253.000
20.150 + 0.85 x 1.425 = 1.3610.5750.150 + 0.85 x (0.681 + 0.575) = 1.2183.000
30.150 + 0.85 x 1.218 = 1.1850.150 + 0.85 x 0.681 = 0.7290.150 + 0.85 x (0.591 + 0.575) = 1.1403.000

The values keep changing by smaller amounts and converge to roughly A = 1.16, B = 0.64, C = 1.20. C ranks highest because it receives links from both A and B; A ranks next because C links to it. The sums stay at 3 because every page has at least one outlink.

Hubs and Authorities (HITS)

HITS gives every page two scores. An authority score measures how much useful information a page contains; a hub score measures how well a page points to good authorities. Authorities are pages linked by good hubs, and hubs are pages linking to good authorities, so the two scores reinforce each other in an iterative computation.

authority(p) = sum of hub(q) for pages q linking to p
hub(p)        = sum of authority(q) for pages q linked from p
(normalise after each iteration)

PageRank vs HITS

AspectPageRankHITS
ScoresOne global importance scoreTwo scores: hub and authority
Computed onThe whole web graphA small query-dependent subgraph
StabilityStable, query-independentCan drift with the query and link spam
UseRanking search resultsFinding authoritative pages for a topic

Exam point: compute one or two PageRank iterations for a three-page graph, and explain the difference between hubs and authorities.

children.title: Web Usage Mining
children.body:
What Usage Mining Finds

Web usage mining analyses clickstreams and server logs to understand how people navigate a site. Typical outputs are frequent page combinations, common navigation paths, user segments and predictions of what a visitor will do next. It is the basis of recommender systems, adaptive menus, cache pre-fetching and conversion analysis.

Data Sources

  • Web server logs: IP address, timestamp, URL, referrer, status code, user agent, bytes.
  • Application logs and database queries on the server.
  • Client-side data: JavaScript events, cookies, scroll depth, form abandonment.
  • Proxy and cache logs, which add noise because several users share one IP.

Preprocessing Steps

  1. Data cleaning: remove requests for images, scripts and stylesheets; discard crawler and error requests (status 404, 500).
  2. User identification: use IP address plus user agent plus cookies; fall back to heuristics when cookies are absent.
  3. Session identification: split a user's requests into sessions by a timeout (commonly 30 minutes) or by a referrer change that indicates a new visit.
  4. Path completion: add missing page views that were served from the browser cache, using the referrer and site structure.
  5. Formatting: convert sessions into sequences, feature vectors or a graph suitable for the chosen mining algorithm.

Pattern Discovery

TechniqueQuestion answeredExample output
Association rulesWhich pages are visited together?home and pricing -> signup, support 8%, confidence 62%
Sequential patternsWhich paths are common?home -> pricing -> signup, 12% of sessions
ClusteringWhat kinds of visitors exist?Browsers, comparers, buyers
ClassificationWill this session convert?Model scoring each live session
Statistical analysisHow do segments differ?Bounce rate by traffic source

Example: Association Rules on Sessions

sessions:
  S1: home, pricing, signup
  S2: home, pricing, docs
  S3: home, docs, signup
  S4: home, pricing, signup

rule home, pricing -> signup
support    = 2/4 = 0.50
confidence = 2/3 = 0.67

The rule says that two thirds of sessions that view home and pricing go on to sign up. A site can act on this by putting a signup prompt on the pricing page.

Pattern Analysis and Applications

  • Validate patterns against business metrics (conversion, revenue, retention) rather than only support and confidence.
  • Personalise navigation or recommendations for a predicted user segment.
  • Improve site structure by shortening common paths and removing dead ends.
  • Detect fraud or bots from unusually regular navigation patterns.
  • Tune caching and prefetching from frequent page sequences.

Privacy and Ethics

Usage data is personal data. Sessions should be anonymised, retained only as long as needed, and used within the consent and legal framework that applies. Aggregated patterns are usually acceptable; re-identifying individuals is not.

Exam point: list the five preprocessing steps for web logs in order, then name four pattern-discovery techniques with an example output.

children.title: Text Mining: Concepts and Information Retrieval
children.body:
What Text Mining Is

Text mining discovers patterns and knowledge from unstructured text: documents, emails, reviews, support tickets, web pages. It combines information retrieval, natural language processing, statistics and machine learning. The goal is not to read every document but to extract structure, topics, sentiment, entities and relationships automatically.

Text Mining vs Information Retrieval

AspectInformation retrieval (IR)Text mining
GoalFind documents relevant to a queryDiscover patterns, topics and facts across documents
OutputRanked list of documentsClusters, topics, rules, sentiment scores, extracted entities
UserA person searchingAn analyst or an automated system
ExampleSearch engine results pageWhich product complaints co-occur with refunds?

IR is often a first step for text mining: retrieve the relevant subset, then mine it.

The Text Preprocessing Pipeline

  1. Tokenisation: split text into words, sentences or n-grams. "data-mining" and "data mining" should produce the same tokens.
  2. Normalisation: lowercase, remove punctuation and HTML, standardise numbers and dates.
  3. Stop-word removal: drop very common words (the, is, at) that carry little meaning for the task.
  4. Stemming: reduce words to a crude root by removing suffixes: mining, mines, mined become min. Fast, but the root may not be a word.
  5. Lemmatisation: reduce words to their dictionary form using grammar: better becomes good. Slower, more accurate.
  6. Feature construction: represent each document as a vector of term frequencies, TF-IDF values, n-grams or embeddings.

Stemming vs Lemmatisation

word        stemming      lemmatisation
studies     studi         study
running     run           run
better      better        good
mice        mice          mouse

Bag of Words

The simplest representation ignores word order and treats a document as a multiset of terms. It is surprisingly effective for classification and clustering, but it cannot distinguish "not good" from "good" and loses phrase structure. N-grams (pairs or triples of words) partly recover the missing context.

Measuring Retrieval Quality

precision = relevant retrieved / retrieved
recall    = relevant retrieved / all relevant
F1        = 2 P R / (P + R)

A search that returns 10 documents of which 6 are relevant has precision 0.6. If 12 relevant documents exist in the collection, recall is 6/12 = 0.5. Precision and recall trade off against each other as the result list grows.

Why Text Is Hard

  • Ambiguity: "bank" is a river edge or a financial institution.
  • Synonymy: "car" and "automobile" mean the same thing but share no letters.
  • High dimensionality: a vocabulary of 100,000 terms gives 100,000 features.
  • Sparsity: a single document contains only a tiny fraction of the vocabulary.
  • Informal language: abbreviations, emoji, spelling errors and sarcasm.
  • Multilingual content and code-mixed text.

Exam point: list the preprocessing steps in order, distinguish stemming from lemmatisation with examples, and define precision and recall for retrieval.

children.title: TF-IDF and the Inverted Index
children.body:
Term Frequency

A term that appears often in a document is likely important for that document. Raw counts favour long documents, so frequency is usually normalised by document length:

tf(t, d) = count of t in d / total terms in d

or the log form: tf = 1 + log10(count)

Inverse Document Frequency

A term that appears in every document is useless for telling documents apart. IDF down-weights common terms and boosts rare ones:

idf(t) = log10( N / df(t) )

N     = number of documents
df(t) = number of documents containing t

df = N    -> idf = 0        (term everywhere)
df = 1    -> idf = log10 N  (term is unique to one document)

TF-IDF Weight

The weight of a term in a document is the product of the two:

w(t, d) = tf(t, d) * idf(t)

TF-IDF gives a high weight to terms that are frequent in a document but rare across the collection. Each document becomes a sparse vector, and documents can be compared with cosine similarity.

Worked Example

Four documents: D1 = "data mining data", D2 = "data science", D3 = "mining science", D4 = "machine learning". N = 4.

Termdfidf = log10(4/df)
data20.301
mining20.301
science20.301
machine10.602
learning10.602
DocumentTermtftf-idf
D1data2/3 = 0.6670.201
D1mining1/3 = 0.3330.100
D2data1/2 = 0.5000.151
D2science0.5000.151
D3mining0.5000.151
D3science0.5000.151
D4machine0.5000.301
D4learning0.5000.301

Cosine similarity between D1 and D2: dot product = 0.201 x 0.151 = 0.030; |D1| = 0.224, |D2| = 0.213; cosine = 0.030 / (0.224 x 0.213) = 0.63. D1 and D2 share "data", so they are fairly similar even though their lengths differ.

The Inverted Index

Scanning every document for every query is impossible at web scale. An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents (and positions) that contain it, so a query only touches the postings of its terms.

data     -> D1: {1, 3}, D2: {1}
mining   -> D1: {2},     D3: {1}
science  -> D2: {2},     D3: {2}
machine  -> D4: {1}
learning -> D4: {2}

query "data science":
  candidates = postings(data) intersect postings(science) = {D2}
  rank D2 by TF-IDF or cosine

Building and Using the Index

  1. Tokenise and normalise every document.
  2. For each term, append the document id and position to its postings list.
  3. Store the dictionary (terms) and postings in a compressed structure.
  4. At query time, intersect postings lists for AND queries, union for OR queries, then rank by TF-IDF or BM25.
  • The dictionary can be hashed or stored as a trie to handle prefixes and spelling variants.
  • Postings lists are kept sorted so intersections are linear in the smaller list.
  • Stop-word removal shrinks the index, but it can remove meaningful terms in phrase queries.

Exam point: compute TF, IDF and TF-IDF for a tiny collection, explain why IDF is needed, and draw an inverted index with positions.

children.title: Text Classification, Clustering and Sentiment Analysis
children.body:
Text Classification

Once documents are vectors, any classifier can be applied: naive Bayes, logistic regression, support vector machines, k-NN or a neural network. Text classification is used for spam filtering, topic labelling, language detection, intent detection and support-ticket routing.

Naive Bayes for Text

The multinomial naive Bayes model treats each document as a bag of words and estimates the probability of each word given the class. With Laplace smoothing:

P(class | words) proportional to P(class) * product over words P(word | class)
P(word | class) = (count(word, class) + 1) / (total words in class + vocabulary size)

It is fast, needs little training data and works well for topic and spam classification. Its independence assumption is clearly false for language, yet the ranking of classes is often still correct.

Support Vector Machines for Text

An SVM finds the boundary that maximises the margin between classes. With TF-IDF vectors and a linear kernel it is a strong baseline for text: high-dimensional sparse data is exactly where linear SVMs excel. Training is slower than naive Bayes but usually more accurate.

Text Clustering

Clustering groups documents without labels. k-means on TF-IDF vectors is common; hierarchical clustering shows topic structure at several levels; topic models such as LDA discover latent themes as distributions over words. Cosine distance is preferred over Euclidean because document length should not dominate.

Topic Modelling with LDA

Latent Dirichlet Allocation assumes that each document is a mixture of topics and each topic is a distribution over words. It returns, for every topic, its most probable words, and for every document, its topic proportions. The number of topics is chosen by the analyst and validated by interpretability.

Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment analysis classifies the attitude expressed in text: positive, negative or neutral, sometimes with intensity. Two approaches:

  • Lexicon-based: sum the polarity of words from a sentiment dictionary, handling negation ("not good") and intensifiers ("very good"). Transparent, but domain-dependent.
  • Machine learning: train a classifier on labelled reviews using n-grams and TF-IDF, or fine-tune a transformer model. More accurate when labelled data exists.

Features that matter: negation scope, contrast ("good but expensive"), sarcasm, emoji, star ratings and aspect terms (battery, screen, service). Evaluation uses the same precision, recall and F1 as any classifier.

Challenges in Text Mining

ChallengeExampleMitigation
Negation"not recommended" scored positive by a bag of wordsNegation detection, n-grams
Sarcasm"great, it broke in a day"Context models, review metadata
Domain shiftMedical terms in a general sentiment lexiconDomain-specific lexicon or retraining
Class imbalanceFew negative reviews among thousandsResampling, threshold tuning
Language mixingHindi-English code-mixed reviewsMultilingual models, transliteration

Exam point: explain naive Bayes for text with the smoothing formula, compare it with an SVM, and describe a sentiment analysis pipeline from raw review to score.

children.title: Mining Complex and Streaming Data
children.body:
Why Classic Algorithms Need Changing

Association, classification and clustering assume a dataset that fits on disk, can be scanned repeatedly, and does not change while it is being mined. Modern applications violate all three assumptions. The patterns must be found in one pass, under memory limits, while the data distribution itself changes over time.

Stream Mining

A data stream is a continuous, potentially unbounded sequence of records (sensor readings, clicks, transactions). Stream mining keeps a compact summary instead of the raw data:

  • Windowed processing: keep only the last N records or the last time period (sliding, tumbling or landmark windows).
  • Sampling and sketching: reservoir sampling, count-min sketch and HyperLogLog estimate frequencies with bounded memory.
  • Incremental models: update the model as each record arrives instead of retraining from scratch.
  • Concept drift: when the relationship between inputs and target changes, detect it (error rate rises) and adapt (reweight, retrain or reset).

Time-Series Mining

Time-series mining looks for trends, seasonality, cycles and anomalies, and for motifs (repeated shapes). Methods include moving averages, ARIMA models, dynamic time warping for similarity, spectral methods and segmentation. Key tasks: forecasting, anomaly detection and classification of sequences.

Graph and Social-Network Mining

  • Community detection: find densely connected groups (Louvain, label propagation).
  • Centrality: degree, betweenness, closeness and PageRank to rank influential nodes.
  • Link prediction: estimate whether two nodes will connect.
  • Frequent subgraph mining: find structural patterns that repeat.
  • Influence maximisation: choose seeds that spread information furthest.

Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Mining

Spatial data adds location (and often time): points, lines and regions. Tasks include spatial clustering (DBSCAN with coordinates), hotspot detection, spatial association rules ("near a school and a bus stop"), co-location patterns and trajectory analysis. Distance is measured geographically, and results must respect map topology.

Multimedia and Text-Rich Mining

Images, audio and video require learned features instead of hand-built attributes. Convolutional networks extract visual features, audio spectrograms are treated as images, and multimodal models combine text, image and audio signals. The mining tasks remain classification, clustering, retrieval and anomaly detection, but the feature engineering is learned.

Privacy-Preserving Mining

  • Anonymisation and k-anonymity: generalise or suppress quasi-identifiers so each record is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others.
  • Differential privacy: add calibrated noise so that query results change little whether or not any single record is present.
  • Federated learning: train a shared model while data stays on each device.
  • Secure computation: compute aggregates across parties without revealing raw records.

Responsible Data Mining

A pattern can be statistically valid and still harmful or illegal. Practitioners check for bias against groups, avoid mining on data collected without consent, document the provenance and limits of models, and provide explanations and appeal routes where decisions affect people.

Exam point: name four modern data types (streams, time series, graphs, spatial), one task and one challenge for each, and two privacy-preserving techniques.

children.title: Important Definitions and Quick Revision
children.body:
Important Definitions

  • Association rule: an implication X -> Y between disjoint itemsets.
  • Support: the fraction of transactions containing X union Y.
  • Confidence: support(X union Y) / support(X); the reliability of the rule.
  • Lift: confidence / support(Y); above 1 means positive association.
  • Frequent itemset: an itemset whose support is at least minsup.
  • Apriori property: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent; every superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent.
  • Candidate itemset: an itemset proposed for counting but not yet confirmed frequent.
  • FP-tree: a compressed prefix tree of transactions used by FP-growth.
  • Conditional pattern base: the set of prefix paths ending at an item, with their counts.
  • Closed itemset: a frequent itemset with no superset of the same support.
  • Maximal itemset: a frequent itemset with no frequent superset.
  • Sequential pattern: a frequent ordered sequence of itemsets.
  • Web content mining: mining the text and media of web pages.
  • Web structure mining: mining the hyperlink graph.
  • Web usage mining: mining logs and clickstreams.
  • PageRank: a link-based importance score, PR(A) = (1-d) + d sum PR(T)/C(T).
  • HITS: an algorithm that computes hub and authority scores.
  • Session: a sequence of page requests by one user within a timeout.
  • Text mining: discovering patterns from unstructured text.
  • Tokenisation: splitting text into words or other units.
  • Stop word: a very common word removed before mining.
  • Stemming: reducing words to a crude root by suffix removal.
  • Lemmatisation: reducing words to their dictionary form.
  • TF-IDF: term frequency times inverse document frequency.
  • Inverted index: a mapping from terms to the documents containing them.
  • Sentiment analysis: classifying the attitude expressed in text.

Important Formulas

support(X -> Y)    = count(X u Y) / N
confidence(X -> Y) = count(X u Y) / count(X)
lift(X -> Y)       = confidence / support(Y)
leverage           = support(X u Y) - support(X) support(Y)
conviction         = (1 - support(Y)) / (1 - confidence)
PageRank(A)        = (1 - d) + d sum ( PR(T) / C(T) )
tf(t, d)           = count(t, d) / |d|
idf(t)             = log10( N / df(t) )
tf-idf             = tf * idf
cosine similarity  = (x . y) / (|x| |y|)

Study Strategy

  • Practise the support, confidence and lift calculations on a small transaction table until they are automatic.
  • Memorise the Apriori property and be able to show at least one candidate pruned by subset and one by count.
  • Draw the FP-tree for the same five transactions so the two algorithms can be compared directly.
  • Remember the three web mining branches and one task per branch; examiners often ask for the taxonomy first.
  • Practise one PageRank iteration by hand; the formula with the damping factor is usually tested.
  • Learn the text pipeline order and the TF-IDF formula; numerical questions are common.
  • Use one running example (market basket or product reviews) across all topics so the answers stay concrete.
  • Revise the differences: Apriori vs FP-growth, closed vs maximal, content vs structure vs usage, stemming vs lemmatisation.
